distractorExplanations.b: Extends the bank exclusion to a subsidiary; the firm that effects trades for the public must itself be the bank to be excluded.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a name printed on a confirmation as the legal test; ownership and branding do not turn the subsidiary into a bank.
distractorExplanations.d: Misreads the activity; effecting trades for the public is broker-dealer business even when no separate advice fee is charged.

prompt: Clearwater Brokerage has no place of business in State F. It effects trades there for banks and insurance companies, and for one State F resident who buys and sells for his own account and meets the accredited-investor tests. Under the Uniform Securities Act, what is Clearwater's duty in State F?

options.text: No registration, because an accredited investor is an institutional buyer under the exclusion
Clearwater must register in State F, because that individual falls outside the institutional exclusion
Register only if Clearwater solicited him, not if he asked to open the account himself
Make a notice filing in place of registration, because adding one accredited customer changes a broker-dealer into a notice-filing firm

explanation: The no-office exclusion applies only when every counterparty in the state is an issuer, another broker-dealer, or a listed institution such as a bank or an insurance company. An individual trading for himself is outside that group. Meeting accredited-investor tests does not, by itself, make him an institutional buyer, so Clearwater must register in State F.

distractorExplanations.a: Equates accreditation with institutional status; those offering tests do not place an individual inside the broker-dealer exclusion.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses solicitation as the dividing line; who proposed the account does not matter once the customer is a resident individual.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a notice-filing category for broker-dealers; one individual customer creates a registration duty, not a substitute filing.

prompt: On April 3, Redwood Securities files a complete broker-dealer application in State N, including the consent to service of process. No proceeding is pending, and the Administrator sets no earlier effective date. On April 10 a salesperson wants to telephone State N residents and solicit securities orders. Under the Uniform Securities Act, what is permitted?

options.text: Those calls on April 10, because a complete application is effective on the filing date
Calls to institutions on April 10, while everyone else must wait for a signed approval order from the Administrator
The salesperson may not solicit State N residents until noon on the 30th day after the April 3 filing
Those calls on April 10 if each prospect already holds a brokerage account at some other firm and is only being asked to transfer it

explanation: Unless a proceeding is pending or the Administrator sets an earlier date, broker-dealer registration becomes effective at noon on the 30th day after a complete application is filed. Redwood filed on April 3, so on April 10 the registration is not effective and the firm may not solicit State N residents.

distractorExplanations.a: Moves effectiveness up to the filing date; noon on the 30th day means April 10 is still inside the waiting period.
distractorExplanations.b: Demands a signed approval order the statute does not require, and a pending applicant may not solicit early by limiting calls to institutions.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents an exception for prospects who already have an account elsewhere; the firm still may not solicit before its registration is effective.

prompt: Summit Street Securities became registered as a broker-dealer in State H during March. It is still effecting trades for State H residents in late December and does not file a renewal. Under the Uniform Securities Act, what is true on January 1?

options.text: Summit stays registered until the Administrator accepts a withdrawal filing
Summit stays registered, because an initial registration runs through the following spring
Summit may keep effecting trades for people who already have accounts, but it must stop opening new ones after the calendar year changes
Summit is not registered in State H, because the registration expired on December 31

explanation: Under the Uniform Securities Act, a broker-dealer registration expires on December 31 unless the firm renews it. Summit did not renew, so on January 1 it is not registered in State H and may not continue effecting trades there until it is registered again.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses expiration with withdrawal; the registration lapses at year-end even though the firm never filed a withdrawal.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents an extension into the spring; an unrenewed registration ends on December 31.
distractorExplanations.c: Saves existing accounts from the lapse; after expiration the firm may not keep effecting trades for anyone in the state.

prompt: Brookline Partners withdrew its broker-dealer registration in State D, and that withdrawal is already effective. Eight months later the Administrator learns that, while registered, the firm sold unregistered nonexempt securities to State D residents. Under the Uniform Securities Act, what may the Administrator do?

options.text: Start a proceeding on that conduct, because 1 year of jurisdiction remains after withdrawal
Take no action, because an effective withdrawal ended the Administrator's authority that same day
Proceed only if Brookline voluntarily files a new registration application in State D
Offer the buyers rescission by letter and stop, because an effective withdrawal bars any proceeding and any findings of fact

explanation: After withdrawal is effective, the Administrator may still begin a suspension or revocation proceeding within 1 year for a willful violation committed while the firm was registered. Selling unregistered nonexempt securities is that kind of violation, and eight months is inside the window, so a proceeding may be started.

distractorExplanations.b: Cuts off authority on the effective date; for a willful violation while the firm was registered, the Act leaves 1 year to start a proceeding.
distractorExplanations.c: Conditions enforcement on a new application; the Administrator does not need the firm's consent or a fresh registration to proceed.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes a rescission letter for a proceeding with written findings; withdrawal does not bar a case on sales made while the firm was registered.

prompt: On June 15, Northbridge Securities, a broker-dealer registered in State T, will merge into a newly formed legal entity that will carry on the same securities business. The new entity has not transacted with anyone yet. Under the Uniform Securities Act, which statement is accurate?

options.text: The new entity becomes registered on its own when the merger closes on June 15
The new entity may apply to succeed to the State T registration for the rest of the year
The new entity may use Northbridge's registration until December 31 and need not file anything
The new entity cannot be registered at all until the next calendar year, because a registration cannot be continued by any successor filing

explanation: The Uniform Securities Act lets a successor broker-dealer apply for registration covering the unexpired portion of the year. The June 15 merger does not register the new entity by itself. Until that successor registration is effective, the new entity may not transact business as a broker-dealer in State T.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the merger as self-executing; a new legal entity is not registered merely because the closing occurred on June 15.
distractorExplanations.c: Skips the successor application; the new entity may not keep using the old registration with no filing.
distractorExplanations.d: Blocks a mid-year registration; a successor application can cover the unexpired portion of the current year.

prompt: Marlow and Dean, a registered broker-dealer, cannot pay its clearing firm or its rent as those bills come due, and its liabilities exceed its assets. Management asks to remain registered while it looks for a buyer. Under the Uniform Securities Act, what may the Administrator do?

options.text: Nothing, until a bankruptcy court has entered an order concerning the firm
Nothing about the registration, because unpaid bills are outside the Act's grounds
Suspend or revoke the registration, because the firm is insolvent under the Act
Leave the registration untouched if management writes that a future buyer will eventually satisfy the clearing firm and the landlord

explanation: The Administrator may suspend or revoke a broker-dealer's registration if the firm is insolvent. Insolvency includes being unable to meet obligations as they come due, which describes the unpaid clearing and rent bills, and it also includes liabilities that exceed assets. A search for a buyer does not remove that ground.

distractorExplanations.a: Defers to a bankruptcy court; the Administrator may act on insolvency under the Act without waiting for a court decree.
distractorExplanations.b: Denies a statutory ground; inability to pay obligations as they come due is insolvency and supports action against the registration.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes a promise about a future buyer for present solvency; the firm is insolvent now, which is enough to suspend or revoke.

prompt: State R's Administrator is reviewing a first broker-dealer application. The principals have passed the required examinations and finished the required training, but none has operated a broker-dealer before. The Administrator wants to deny the application solely for that lack of experience. Under the Uniform Securities Act, is the denial permitted?

options.text: Yes, a first-time firm must be denied until its principals have operated a broker-dealer before
Yes, if the firm will not post a surety bond, because a bond is what removes an experience objection
Yes, but only during the firm's first calendar year, after which the denial has to be lifted whether or not anything else has changed
No, the denial is not permitted, because lack of experience alone is not a ground when training or knowledge is shown

explanation: The Uniform Securities Act does not allow a denial based solely on lack of experience when the applicant is qualified by training, knowledge, or both. Passing the required examinations and completing the required training supplies that qualification, so this proposed denial is not permitted.

distractorExplanations.a: Makes prior operating experience a prerequisite; the Act forbids a denial that rests only on lack of experience when training or knowledge is present.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats a surety bond as a cure for inexperience; the limit on an experience-only denial does not depend on whether a bond is discussed.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a one-year denial that later lifts itself; the Administrator may not enter the experience-only denial in the first place.

prompt: The last known officer of a registered broker-dealer cannot be located after a reasonable search. The firm has dissolved and has ceased doing business. No misconduct is alleged. Under the Uniform Securities Act, which action fits these facts?

options.text: Cancel the registration, because the firm has dissolved, ceased business, and cannot be located
Revoke the registration for fraud, because winding a firm up always requires a finding of willful misconduct
Leave the registration in force until December 31, because nobody has filed a withdrawal
Suspend the registration for a set disciplinary term even though the Administrator has not alleged any violation of the Act

explanation: The Administrator may cancel a broker-dealer registration when the firm is no longer in existence, has ceased to do business, or cannot be located after a reasonable search. Cancellation closes the record. It is not a revocation, and it does not require a finding that anyone committed misconduct.

distractorExplanations.b: Uses revocation without a ground; revocation is a sanction that needs statutory findings, and no misconduct is alleged on these facts.
distractorExplanations.c: Waits for year-end or a withdrawal form; cancellation is available now because the firm has dissolved and cannot be located.
distractorExplanations.d: Turns a record close-out into discipline; a suspension needs a statutory ground, which these facts do not supply.

prompt: A dentist who lives in State Y mails a sell order to a broker-dealer that has no place of business in State Y. The firm has never solicited her, or anyone else, in State Y. She is selling shares she already owns, for her own account. Under the Uniform Securities Act, what must the firm do before it executes that order?

options.text: Execute it, because an unsolicited order from a resident individual is excluded
The firm must register in State Y as a broker-dealer before executing this order
Execute it if the shares are listed on an exchange, because the listing registers the firm in her state
Execute this order now, and register in State Y only if she mails a second order later in the same year

explanation: Executing a securities order for a resident individual is transacting business as a broker-dealer in her state. The firm has no place of business in State Y, and she is not an institution, so the institutional exclusion does not apply. An unsolicited order can matter for some securities-registration exemptions; it does not excuse the firm's own registration.

distractorExplanations.a: Borrows an unsolicited-order concept from securities registration and applies it to the firm; the broker-dealer still has to be registered.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses exchange listing, which can make a security federal covered, with registration of the broker-dealer that effects the trade.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a second-order threshold; the first transaction for a resident individual requires registration before it is executed.

prompt: Halcyon Securities is registered as a broker-dealer in State A, where its only office is located. Residents of State J can open its public website. Halcyon has no place of business in State J, has no customers there, and has not offered securities to anyone in State J. Under the Uniform Securities Act, must Halcyon register in State J?

options.text: Yes, because a website that residents can open is a place of business in their state
Yes, because any public website requires broker-dealer registration in every state whose residents might read it
No, Halcyon need not register, because it has no State J office and no securities business there
No if the site blocks State J addresses, but if residents can open the page then each view is an offer and registration is required before anyone in State J reads it

explanation: A broker-dealer must register in a state where it has a place of business or where it transacts securities business with retail residents, including offers directed to them. A website people can open is not itself a place of business. Halcyon has no State J office, no State J customers, and has not offered securities to anyone there, so State J registration is not required.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a generally available website as an office; on these facts Halcyon has no place of business in State J.
distractorExplanations.b: Turns a public website into nationwide registration; a state with no office and no securities business is not an automatic registration.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a page view as an offer directed into State J; the firm has not offered securities to anyone there.

prompt: A customer phones her agent: "Buy 300 shares of XYZ for me today, and use your judgment on the price." She has never signed a discretionary authorization. What may the agent do under the NASAA Statement of Policy on dishonest or unethical practices?

options.text: Decline the order until the customer signs and returns a written discretionary authorization form
Enter the order today, choosing the time and price, without written discretionary authority
Buy XYZ or a similar stock in the same industry if XYZ looks overpriced during the day
Enter the order now and obtain her written authorization within 10 business days

explanation: The Statement of Policy bars exercising discretion without prior written authority, but discretion that relates solely to the time and/or price of execution is excluded. The customer chose the security, the action and the quantity, so the agent may pick the timing and price. Under FINRA Rule 3260 that time-and-price authority lapses at the end of the business day it was given.

distractorExplanations.a: Over-applies the written-authority rule; time-and-price discretion is carved out, so no signed discretionary form is needed for this order.
distractorExplanations.c: Choosing a different security is true discretion over the asset itself, which requires prior written authority the customer never gave.
distractorExplanations.d: Borrows the IA model rule's 10-business-day window for oral discretion; it is not needed here and does not apply to a broker-dealer agent.

prompt: Over six months, an agent turned over a retired customer's $150,000 conservative income account about eight times. Every trade was solicited and approved by the customer, and commissions equaled roughly 18% of the account. Which violation does this pattern most clearly indicate?

options.text: Unauthorized trading, because solicited trades need written discretionary authority
Front-running, because the agent placed firm orders ahead of the customer's orders
Market manipulation, because the volume of trades moved the prices of the securities
Churning, because trading was excessive in size and frequency for this account

explanation: Churning is inducing trading that is excessive in size or frequency in view of the customer's financial resources and the character of the account. High turnover and commissions consuming about 18% of a conservative retiree's account are classic signs, and customer approval of each solicited trade does not cure it.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses churning with unauthorized trading; the customer approved each solicited trade, so no discretionary authority was exercised.
distractorExplanations.b: Front-running means trading ahead of a customer's block order to profit from it; nothing in the facts shows firm orders placed first.
distractorExplanations.c: Manipulation requires trading designed to create false price or volume signals; trades in one retail account are not shown to move prices.

Quoting a distribution rate before the REIT's prospectus had been delivered to her
Selling a security that is not listed on any national securities exchange to a retiree

A discretionary-account client, provided the loan is repaid within 30 days

prompt: A customer invites her agent to share in the profits and losses of her trading account, and the agent will contribute 25% of the money in it. Which arrangement is permissible?

The agent shares 25% of gains and losses after telling the branch manager orally
The agent shares 25% of gains and losses with prior written consent of customer and firm

explanation: Sharing in a customer account requires prior written authorization from the customer and from the employing firm, and the agent's share of gains and losses must be in proportion to the agent's contribution (FINRA Rule 2150; NASAA treats unauthorized sharing as unethical). Permitted, because the stock rose and the customer suffered no loss from the promise

options.text: In the context of the whole portfolio and its overall risk-and-return strategy
On its own merits, so a speculative holding is imprudent regardless of the rest
By whether that position produced a gain during the trustee's time in office
By whether the beneficiaries approved the specific investment in writing first

explanation: The Uniform Prudent Investor Act judges each investment as part of the overall portfolio and a strategy with risk and return objectives suited to the trust, not in isolation. No category of investment is imprudent per se, diversification is required absent special circumstances, and duties may be delegated with care in selecting and monitoring the agent.

distractorExplanations.b: Reflects the old prudent-man approach of judging assets one by one; the Act rejects per se imprudence for any category.
distractorExplanations.c: Prudence is measured by the decision process at the time, not by hindsight results for a single position.
distractorExplanations.d: Beneficiary pre-approval is not the prudence standard; the trustee must meet the Act's duties regardless of approval.

Travel and hotel costs for the adviser's staff to attend an industry conference
Third-party research reports the adviser uses in making client investment decisions
Office furniture and the salaries of the adviser's administrative support staff

explanation: Section 28(e) protects an adviser that pays higher commissions in good faith for brokerage and research services that assist its investment decision-making, such as research reports and analytical tools. Overhead that benefits the adviser rather than clients falls outside, and soft-dollar arrangements must be disclosed to clients.

distractorExplanations.a: Office rent is general overhead that benefits the adviser's business, not research or brokerage services under 28(e).
distractorExplanations.b: Travel and lodging are excluded from the safe harbor even when the conference covers investment topics.
distractorExplanations.d: Furniture and administrative salaries are overhead expenses the adviser must pay itself, outside the 28(e) safe harbor.

prompt: An agent with no written discretionary authority sees a stock drop 12% before the open and buys 200 shares for a customer who has owned it for years, planning to call her at lunch. The customer had never discussed adding to the position. How is the trade classified?

options.text: A permitted time-and-price discretion order, because the customer already owns the stock and the agent picked only the price
An unauthorized transaction, because the customer never approved this specific trade
Acceptable if the agent confirms it with the customer the same day
Acceptable because the purchase is suitable for an existing holder

explanation: Without written discretionary authority, an agent may act only on the customer's instruction for the specific security, buy or sell, and quantity. Entering a trade the customer never discussed is an unauthorized transaction, an unethical practice under NASAA rules regardless of how sensible the trade looks.

distractorExplanations.a: Time-and-price discretion still needs the customer to choose the security, the action and the amount; here she chose nothing.
distractorExplanations.c: Calling after the fact does not cure the violation; approval had to come before the order was entered.
distractorExplanations.d: Suitability and authority are separate tests: a suitable trade placed without authority is still unauthorized.

prompt: Two agents at different firms coordinate so that one enters buy orders and the other enters matching sell orders in the same thinly traded stock at the same price, with no change in beneficial ownership between their related accounts. What is this practice?

options.text: Legitimate crossing of customer orders, because both sides trade at the prevailing market price and no customer is harmed
Churning, because the trades create commissions without benefit to customers
Front-running, because the agents knew of each other's orders in advance
Matched orders, a form of market manipulation that creates false trading activity

explanation: Prearranged buy and sell orders entered at the same time and price to create the appearance of active trading are matched orders; when no beneficial ownership changes they are also wash trades. Both are manipulative practices prohibited under the Uniform Securities Act and NASAA's dishonest and unethical practices rules.

distractorExplanations.a: Crossing is legitimate only for genuine, independent customer orders; prearranged trades between related accounts only paint the tape.
distractorExplanations.b: Churning is excessive trading in a customer account; this scheme fakes volume to mislead the market.
distractorExplanations.c: Front-running means trading ahead of a customer's block order for one's own benefit, not prearranging matching trades.

prompt: An agent receives a customer's order to buy 80,000 shares of a mid-cap stock, an order large enough to move the price. Before entering it, the agent buys 2,000 shares for his own account. What has the agent done?

options.text: Interpositioning, because a second party stood between the customer and the market
Nothing improper, as long as the customer's order is filled the same day
Front-running, trading ahead of a customer's block order on that knowledge
Insider trading, because the agent used material nonpublic information about the issuer to buy the shares

explanation: Front-running is trading for one's own (or the firm's) account with advance knowledge of a customer's block order that is likely to move the price. It puts the agent's interest ahead of the customer's and is a prohibited unethical practice.

distractorExplanations.a: Interpositioning inserts another dealer into the trade to add cost; here the agent traded ahead for himself.
distractorExplanations.b: Same-day execution does not cure the abuse; the agent profited from advance knowledge of the customer's order.
distractorExplanations.d: The information concerns a pending customer order, not the issuer's business; the correct name is front-running.

prompt: A customer hands her agent a $25,000 check to fund a new brokerage account. To save a trip, the agent deposits it into his personal checking account and wires the money to the firm three days later. Which violation has occurred?

No violation, because the funds reached the customer's account within a week
Misappropriation only if the agent earned interest on the money

distractorExplanations.c: The prohibition is on mixing the money at all; prompt delivery afterward does not undo the commingling.
distractorExplanations.d: Earning interest would add misappropriation, but commingling occurs as soon as customer funds go into the agent's account.

Prior written client consent after full disclosure, and no recommendation of the trade to both sides

distractorExplanations.b: After-the-fact disclosure is not enough; written consent must be obtained in advance.

prompt: A state-registered adviser's contract says the adviser "shall not be liable for any loss arising from its advice, and the client waives all claims against the adviser." How do NASAA rules treat this clause?

options.text: As a prohibited hedge clause that misleads clients into thinking they gave up legal rights
As acceptable only for clients who are accredited investors
As valid if the adviser also discloses its conflicts of interest and the client initials the clause separately
As valid, because the client signed the contract voluntarily

explanation: Any contract provision that purports to waive a client's rights under securities law, or that suggests the client cannot sue, is a prohibited hedge clause. Advisers may describe reasonable limits on their duties, but they cannot imply the client gave up legal remedies.

distractorExplanations.b: Investor sophistication does not make a waiver of statutory rights enforceable or permitted.
distractorExplanations.c: Disclosure of conflicts does not cure a clause suggesting the client waived nonwaivable rights.
distractorExplanations.d: A signature cannot waive the protections of securities law, so the clause stays prohibited.

As unethical, because the agent failed to follow the customer's order promptly

prompt: A household uses two firms. An investment adviser representative manages its fee-based portfolio. A broker-dealer agent at the other firm only enters orders the household sends unsolicited and makes no recommendation. Under NASAA's unethical-practices rule for advisers, who must act primarily for this household's benefit?

options.text: The investment adviser representative, whom that adviser rule treats as a fiduciary
The broker-dealer agent, because entering an unsolicited order is treated as advice that creates the same duty
Both the representative and the agent, because anyone the household pays for a securities service is a fiduciary
Neither person, because a fiduciary duty arises only after the household signs a waiver of every conflict of interest

explanation: NASAA's unethical-practices rule for advisers says an investment adviser representative is a fiduciary and must act primarily for the client's benefit. The representative managing this portfolio is in that group. An agent who only enters unsolicited orders is outside that adviser rule and does not become a fiduciary by taking those orders.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats unsolicited order entry as advice. Taking an order the household already chose does not place a broker-dealer agent under the adviser fiduciary rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Extends the fiduciary label to every paid securities role. The adviser rule attaches that duty to advisers and their representatives, not to every agent.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses how the duty arises. The rule imposes it because the person is an adviser representative, and a conflict waiver does not create the duty.

prompt: Two share classes of one bond fund both fit a client's income objective and risk limits. The cheaper class pays the investment adviser representative nothing beyond the advisory fee. The costlier class pays that representative an extra ongoing fee. What does the representative's fiduciary duty require?

options.text: Buy the costlier class, because the extra ongoing fee shows the fund family is more committed to the client
Buy the cheaper class, putting the client's benefit ahead of the representative's extra fee
Buy the costlier class if the extra fee is mentioned in the following year's brochure update
Make no recommendation at all, because any fee gap cancels the duty of loyalty and leaves the entire choice with the client

explanation: NASAA's adviser rule makes the representative a fiduciary who must act primarily for the client's benefit. The two classes serve the same objective, so choosing the class that pays the representative an extra fee puts that conflict ahead of the client. Naming the fee in a later brochure does not repair the choice.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the representative's extra fee as a reason to prefer the costlier class. That inverts the duty of loyalty, which requires the client's benefit to come first.
distractorExplanations.c: Postpones disclosure until next year's brochure and still selects the conflicted class. Loyalty is not satisfied by a late mention of a fee the representative chose to keep.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a fee difference as canceling the duty of loyalty. The duty requires a recommendation that favors the client, not silence in the face of two unequal classes.

prompt: An investment adviser representative is preparing to recommend that a client buy shares of one public company. The representative's spouse already holds a large personal block of that same company, and a reasonable client would want to know. Under NASAA's prohibited-conduct rule for advisers, when must this conflict be disclosed?

options.text: In the firm's next annual amendment, which is early enough for a household holding the representative did not buy personally
Only if the client first asks whether anyone in the representative's household owns that company
In writing before any advice is rendered, so the client can weigh the conflict first
After the trade settles, inside the confirmation the custodian sends to every purchasing client

explanation: NASAA's prohibited-conduct rule for advisers requires a material conflict of interest to be disclosed in writing before any advice is rendered. A spouse's large holding in the company about to be recommended would matter to a reasonable client. An annual amendment, a client question, or a confirmation after the purchase comes too late.

distractorExplanations.a: Delays a material conflict until the next annual amendment. The rule requires written disclosure before the advice, not in a later filing about a holding the representative did not buy.
distractorExplanations.b: Shifts the duty onto the client to ask. The representative must disclose the spouse's block without waiting for a question about household ownership.
distractorExplanations.d: Moves disclosure to a confirmation after the trade settles. By then the client has already acted on advice that hid a material conflict.

prompt: A client with a stated growth objective, and with savings much larger than the order, accepts one solicited purchase of a diversified equity fund. The agent earns an ordinary commission and suggests no further trades. How does NASAA's broker-dealer policy classify this order?

options.text: As churning, because every solicited purchase that pays an agent a commission is excessive in size or frequency
As an unauthorized trade, because a solicited purchase is lawful only when written discretionary authority is already on file
As a fiduciary breach, because earning a commission turns a broker-dealer agent into a fiduciary
As a suitable trade, because one purchase that fits the client's objective is not excessive trading

explanation: NASAA's broker-dealer policy treats churning as inducing trades that are excessive in size or frequency given the customer's financial resources and the character of the account. One solicited purchase that fits a stated growth objective, in an account that can support it, is a suitable trade. An ordinary commission does not make that purchase excessive and does not turn the agent into an adviser fiduciary.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats any commission on a solicited purchase as churning. Churning requires trading that is excessive for the account, and this is a single fitting purchase.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a recommendation the client accepted with discretion. Written discretionary authority is not required when the client agrees to the specific purchase.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a commission as creating an adviser fiduciary duty. This agent made one suitable recommendation and is not acting as an investment adviser.

prompt: A client wrote that the account is for steady income and should remain in high-grade bonds. For many months an agent urges sales of those bonds and purchases of speculative stocks. The client signs each order ticket. Commissions consume a heavy share of the account. Which practice does NASAA's broker-dealer policy describe?

options.text: Churning, because the agent induced trading excessive for this account's resources and character
Sound suitability, because a signature on each ticket proves the speculative stocks fit the income goal
Proper time-and-price discretion, because the client left the timing of each bond sale to the agent
A lawful growth shift, because speculative stocks may replace bonds whenever the client signs the order ticket

explanation: NASAA treats as dishonest the inducing of trading that is excessive in size or frequency in view of the customer's financial resources and the character of the account. Repeated moves from high-grade bonds into speculative stocks contradict an account dedicated to steady income, and the heavy commissions show whose interest the activity served. A signature on each ticket does not cure that inducement.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats the client's signature as proof of suitability. Agreeing to each induced trade does not make speculative stocks fit an account the client limited to high-grade bond income.
distractorExplanations.c: Misreads the activity as time-and-price discretion. The agent chose different securities, not merely when to sell bonds the client had already selected.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a signed ticket as permission to abandon the account's income character. The policy still judges the pattern against that character and the client's resources.

prompt: A client's account form states an objective of active short-term trading, and the client's liquid resources are ample for that style. An agent solicits frequent trades that stay within the written objective and those resources. Under NASAA's test for excessive trading, what follows?

options.text: The trading is churning, because frequent solicited trades are excessive no matter what the account form says
The trading is not churning, because the frequency fits the account's character and the client's resources
The trading is churning unless the client first grants written discretion over every single order
The trading is not churning only when the agent receives no compensation of any kind on the activity

explanation: NASAA's excessive-trading standard looks at size and frequency in view of the customer's financial resources and the character of the account. Frequent trades are not excessive when the account's stated character is active short-term trading and the client's resources support that style. The test does not require written discretion, and it does not forbid ordinary pay on activity the account was opened to pursue.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores the character of the account. Frequency is judged against the stated objective and the client's resources, not against a ban on every solicited trade.
distractorExplanations.c: Imports the discretionary-authority rule into the excessive-trading test. Churning turns on inducement and excess, not on whether a discretion letter is on file.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats any compensation as churning. Ordinary pay on trades that fit the account's character and resources is not what the excessive-trading rule forbids.

prompt: A client asks an agent to exit one concentrated stock and spread the proceeds across several diversified funds. The agent sells that stock and buys the funds during the same week, then enters no further orders. Each fund matches the client's new objective. What is this pattern?

options.text: Churning, because more than one transaction during a single week is always excessive frequency
An unethical fund switch, because leaving any stock for funds is prohibited no matter what the client requested
A suitable reallocation, because the trades carry out one requested change and then stop
Unauthorized trading, because dividing one stock into several funds requires a power of attorney the client never signed

explanation: Churning is induced trading that is excessive in size or frequency given the customer's resources and the character of the account. The client requested one move out of a concentrated stock into diversified funds, the agent completed that move, and the orders then stopped. Those trades are a suitable reallocation, and the client's request is the authority for them.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a one-week implementation as excessive frequency. The policy looks at whether the activity is excessive for the account, and this requested change stopped once it was done.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a requested exit from a concentrated stock with a prohibited mutual-fund switch. The client asked for the new mix, and each fund matches that objective.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a specific client instruction with missing discretionary authority. The client directed this sale and the purchases, so no power of attorney is required.

prompt: An agent holds no discretionary authorization. A conservative client never proposes a trade and accepts every suggestion the same day. Those suggestions produce a rapid series of large trades that overwhelm the client's resources and ignore the account's conservative character. Under NASAA's broker-dealer policy, what is this?

options.text: Lawful conduct, because excessive trading can exist only in an account that already has written discretionary authority
Lawful conduct, because same-day acceptance by the client means the agent did not induce any of the trades
An unethical guarantee of profit, because a rapid series of trades is a promise that the client will gain
Churning, because inducing excessive trading does not require written discretionary authority

explanation: NASAA's broker-dealer policy prohibits inducing trading that is excessive in size or frequency in view of the customer's financial resources and the character of the account. The agent prompted every trade, the client only assented, and the series was too large for a conservative account. Written discretionary authority is a separate rule and is not an element of this prohibition.

distractorExplanations.a: Makes written discretion an element of churning. The excessive-trading ban is about inducement and the account's resources and character, and it applies without a discretion letter.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats rubber-stamp acceptance as proof the agent did not induce the trades. The suggestions prompted the activity, which is inducement even though the client said yes each day.
distractorExplanations.c: Mislabels the pattern as a guarantee against loss or a promise of profit. The violation is excessive trading, and nothing in the facts guarantees a result.

prompt: An agent asks a customer for a personal loan. The customer is a bank and offers the loan on ordinary commercial terms. The agent's only tie to that bank is the brokerage account. Under NASAA's rule for agents, may the agent borrow?

options.text: No. An agent may not borrow money or securities from a customer
Yes. A bank that lends on ordinary commercial terms is a permitted lender to an agent
Yes, once the agent signs a promissory note and repays the loan on the bank's usual schedule
Yes, once the agent's broker-dealer countersigns the note before the bank sends any of the funds

explanation: NASAA's Statement of Policy treats an agent's borrowing of money or securities from a customer as an unethical practice, and the agent paragraph states no exception. Ordinary commercial terms, a promissory note, and a broker-dealer countersignature do not add a lender category for agents. The exception for a financial institution in the business of loaning funds is in the adviser rule, not the agent rule.

distractorExplanations.b: Applies the adviser-rule exception for a lending institution to an agent. The agent rule bans borrowing from a customer and lists no bank exception.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a promissory note and a normal repayment schedule as curing the ban. The agent rule prohibits the loan itself, whatever the paperwork and the repayment terms.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a broker-dealer countersignature as permission. The agent paragraph does not allow the firm to authorize borrowing from a customer.

prompt: An investment adviser representative wants to borrow money from a client. NASAA's adviser rule permits that borrowing from only three kinds of client. Which client is one of those three?

options.text: A longtime individual client who offers the money interest-free and confirms the offer in a signed letter
A client that is a financial institution engaged in the business of loaning funds
The representative's adult child, who opened an advisory account with the firm recently
A client who practices law and regularly drafts loan agreements for other borrowers

explanation: NASAA's adviser rule allows borrowing from a client only when that client is a broker-dealer, an affiliate of the investment adviser, or a financial institution engaged in the business of loaning funds. A client institution in the lending business fits the third category. An individual client, a relative with an account, and a lawyer who drafts loan papers do not.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a willing individual client and a signed letter as an exception. A private client is not a broker-dealer, an affiliate, or a financial institution that loans funds.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a relative who recently became a client as a permitted lender. Family status is not one of the three categories in the adviser borrowing rule.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a lawyer who drafts loan agreements with a financial institution engaged in the business of loaning funds. Drafting documents is not that business.

prompt: An investment adviser representative's brother, who is an advisory client, offers to lend the representative shares from that advisory account so the representative can cover a personal short. The brother is not a broker-dealer, not an affiliate of the adviser, and not in the business of loaning funds. May the representative accept?

options.text: Yes, because a sibling stands outside the borrowing ban that applies to unrelated clients
Yes, if the brother signs an acknowledgment that he understands the conflict before the shares move
No, because this brother is a client and is outside the three permitted lenders
Yes, if a supervisor approves the stock loan in an email before the shares leave the account

explanation: NASAA's adviser rule bars borrowing money or securities from a client unless the client is a broker-dealer, an affiliate of the adviser, or a financial institution engaged in the business of loaning funds. This brother is a client and fits none of those categories, so the shares may not be borrowed. Family ties, a signed acknowledgment, and a supervisor's email do not add a fourth lender.

distractorExplanations.a: Invents a family exception to the adviser borrowing rule. A sibling who is a client is still a client, and the rule lists no relative category.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats a written acknowledgment of the conflict as permission to borrow. Disclosure of the conflict does not place the brother among the three permitted lenders.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a supervisor's email as an exception. Firm approval cannot authorize borrowing securities from a client who is outside the three permitted lenders.

prompt: A state-registered adviser wants to borrow cash from its parent company. The parent is a client of the adviser and an affiliate of the adviser, and it is neither a broker-dealer nor a bank. Under NASAA's adviser borrowing rule, what is the result?

options.text: Prohibited, because the only permitted lender is a financial institution engaged in the business of loaning funds
Prohibited, because an affiliate that is also a client is the one relationship the borrowing rule never allows
Permitted only after every other advisory client consents to the loan in a separate writing
Permitted, because a client that is an affiliate of the adviser is a permitted lender

explanation: NASAA's adviser rule permits borrowing from a client who is a broker-dealer, an affiliate of the investment adviser, or a financial institution engaged in the business of loaning funds. The parent is stated to be both a client and an affiliate, so it is a permitted lender even though it is not a bank or a broker-dealer. Consent from the adviser's other clients is not a condition of that exception.

distractorExplanations.a: Drops two of the three permitted lenders and keeps only the financial institution. An affiliate of the adviser is itself a permitted lender under the same rule.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats the affiliate relationship as a bar. The rule specifically allows borrowing when the client is an affiliate of the investment adviser.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds a consent condition the borrowing exception does not contain. Other clients do not have to approve a loan from an affiliate that is a permitted lender.

prompt: A wealthy advisory client who is a private individual offers an investment adviser representative a loan at a market interest rate and signs a promissory note. The client is not a broker-dealer, not an affiliate of the adviser, and not a lending institution. What is the status of the loan under NASAA's adviser rule?

options.text: Prohibited, because a willing individual is not one of the three permitted lenders
Permitted, because a market interest rate and a signed promissory note remove the conflict of borrowing
Permitted, because the client volunteered the funds, so the representative never solicited the loan
Permitted if the representative repays the full balance before the quarter in which the loan was made has ended

explanation: NASAA allows an adviser or representative to borrow from a client only if the client is a broker-dealer, an affiliate of the adviser, or a financial institution engaged in the business of loaning funds. A private individual is none of those three, so the loan is prohibited. A market rate, a promissory note, a volunteer offer, and fast repayment do not create another exception.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats commercial loan paperwork as an exception. A market rate and a promissory note do not make a private individual one of the three permitted lenders.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the client's initiative as curing the ban. The rule covers the borrowing itself, whether or not the representative asked for the loan.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a repayment deadline as a cure. Paying the loan back quickly does not place a private individual client among the permitted lenders.

prompt: An agent and a customer want the agent to share the customer's trading profits and losses. NASAA permits that sharing only with written authorization from the customer and from the broker-dealer the agent represents. Which arrangement meets those written conditions?

options.text: The customer agrees on a telephone call, and the branch manager nods during a staff meeting
The customer and the broker-dealer each sign a written authorization before sharing begins
The customer signs a written authorization, and the agent tells the broker-dealer orally that same afternoon
The broker-dealer signs a written authorization, and the customer agrees only by a telephone call

explanation: NASAA's rule for agents allows sharing in a customer's profits or losses only when the customer and the broker-dealer the agent represents have both given written authorization. Signed authorizations from each of them satisfy those conditions. A phone call, a nod in a meeting, or an oral report to the firm leaves at least one of the two writings missing.

distractorExplanations.a: Replaces both writings with speech and a nod. The stated rule requires written authorization from the customer and from the broker-dealer, and neither has signed.
distractorExplanations.c: Supplies the customer's writing but only an oral notice to the broker-dealer. The stated rule requires the firm's authorization to be written as well.
distractorExplanations.d: Supplies the broker-dealer's writing but only a telephone yes from the customer. The stated rule requires the customer's authorization to be written as well.

prompt: An agent will take part of a customer's profits, will not share losses, and will contribute no capital. The customer and the broker-dealer have both signed written authorizations. The NASAA agent rule stated here allows sharing in profits or losses only with those two writings and states no further condition. Under that stated rule, which conclusion is right?

options.text: The arrangement is prohibited, because the agent must also contribute capital in the same proportion as the profit share
The arrangement is prohibited, because sharing stays banned even after both written authorizations have been signed
The arrangement is permitted, because both written authorizations the rule states are already in place
The arrangement is prohibited unless the customer is a member of the agent's immediate household

explanation: The NASAA agent rule stated in the stem bars sharing in a customer's profits or losses unless the customer and the broker-dealer have both authorized it in writing. Both writings are signed here, and the stem states no further condition. A matching capital contribution, a ban that survives the writings, and a household limit are not conditions of that stated rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Adds a capital-proportion condition the stem does not state. Under the stated rule, sharing is judged only by whether both written authorizations are in place.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats the sharing ban as surviving the writings. The stated rule allows the sharing once the customer and the broker-dealer have both authorized it in writing.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds a household limit the stated rule does not contain. The two writings are the only conditions the stem gives, and both are already signed.

prompt: An agent's spouse, who is a customer, has signed a written authorization allowing the agent to share that account's profits and losses. The broker-dealer the agent represents has not authorized the sharing in writing. NASAA allows the sharing only when both of those writings exist. What is still required?

options.text: Nothing further, because an account owned by a spouse never needs the broker-dealer's separate writing
Nothing further, because the spouse's signature counts as authorization from both the customer and the firm
A fresh cash contribution by the spouse into the account before any sharing of profits is allowed to start
Written authorization from the broker-dealer, which the stated rule still requires

explanation: NASAA allows an agent to share in a customer's profits and losses only with written authorization from the customer and from the broker-dealer the agent represents. The spouse has signed, but the spouse is still a customer, and the firm's writing is a separate condition. Marriage does not remove the broker-dealer's written authorization.

distractorExplanations.a: Drops the broker-dealer's writing because the customer is a spouse. The stated rule still requires that writing, and marriage is not a substitute for it.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats one signature as both authorizations. The customer and the broker-dealer are different parties, and each must authorize the sharing in writing.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds a cash contribution the stated rule does not require. What is missing is the broker-dealer's written authorization, not new money from the spouse.

prompt: On an unrecorded telephone call, a customer and a broker-dealer principal each tell an agent they agree the agent may share the account's profits and losses. No authorization is signed. NASAA allows that sharing only with written authorization from the customer and from the broker-dealer. What is the result?

options.text: The call is enough, because the principal's spoken agreement stands in for the broker-dealer's written authorization
The call is enough, because the customer's spoken agreement is the only authorization this rule requires from anyone
The call is enough once the agent places a personal note in the file describing what each person said on the phone
The call is not enough, because spoken agreement is not the written authorization the rule requires

explanation: NASAA's agent rule allows sharing in profits or losses only with written authorization from the customer and from the broker-dealer the agent represents. On this call both people spoke and nobody signed, so neither writing exists. A principal's spoken yes, and the agent's own note of the call, are not those written authorizations.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a principal's spoken yes as the broker-dealer's written authorization. The stated rule requires a writing from the firm, and speech on a call is not that writing.
distractorExplanations.b: Drops the broker-dealer's writing and accepts the customer's oral yes. The stated rule requires a written authorization from each of them.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the agent's own file note as the missing writings. A memo the agent writes is not written authorization from the customer or from the broker-dealer.

prompt: On weekends, an agent offers a local factory's promissory notes as investments to three brokerage customers and records the sales only in a home notebook. He is paid nothing, and his broker-dealer has not authorized the notes. Under NASAA's dishonest-practices policy, which statement is correct?

options.text: Those off-book sales are prohibited unless the broker-dealer authorizes them in writing before execution.
Because the agent is unpaid, the notes are a personal matter and need not be authorized by the broker-dealer or recorded on its books.
A phone call to the branch manager after the first weekend sale is enough, since written approval is only for paid outside business activity.
Each customer's signed statement that the note is an investment replaces the broker-dealer's prior written authorization.

explanation: NASAA treats an agent's securities transactions that are missing from the broker-dealer's books as a dishonest practice unless the firm authorizes them in writing before execution. Notes offered to customers as investments are securities transactions. Lack of pay does not remove the duty, and a home notebook is not the firm's record.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the rule with a pay test. NASAA still requires the broker-dealer's prior written authorization when the agent is paid nothing.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a later phone call as enough. The policy requires written authorization before execution, not oral notice after the first sale.
distractorExplanations.d: Mistakes a customer's investment statement for the firm's authorization. That paper does not put the sales on the broker-dealer's books.

prompt: While describing a corporate bond, an agent says it is secured by a first mortgage on the issuer's plant. He has read the prospectus, which shows an unsecured debenture. The bond's price later rises. How should that statement be treated?

options.text: The statement is cured by the later price rise, because a misstatement about collateral counts only when the buyer loses money on the trade.
It is a material misstatement, and the later price rise does not cure the untrue claim about collateral.
It is only a prospectus-delivery issue, because an oral remark about what secures a bond is outside the antifraud rules.
It is harmless emphasis, because a wrong word about the lien is immaterial when the coupon and the maturity were stated correctly.

explanation: NASAA's dishonest-practices standards treat a misstatement of a material fact as grounds for action, and the Uniform Securities Act's antifraud provision bars untrue statements in connection with a securities offer. Whether the bond is mortgage-backed or an unsecured debenture changes the buyer's risk, so the claim is material. A later rise in price does not undo it, and having read the prospectus makes the contradictory oral claim worse, not better.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a later profit as a cure. An untrue statement about collateral is material whether or not the buyer loses money.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a false oral claim with a missing prospectus. The antifraud problem is the untrue statement itself, not merely a delivery failure.
distractorExplanations.d: Misses materiality. Secured versus unsecured status changes credit risk even when the coupon and the maturity were stated correctly.

prompt: Hesitant about a closed-end fund, a customer is told that if she is down after six months, the firm will buy the shares back at her cost. The firm never approved that promise, and the shares later rise. Under NASAA's policy, which statement is correct?

options.text: The promise is allowed, because the firm never approved it and the shares rose, so the customer was never paid on the promise.
The promise is allowed as a market opinion that the closed-end fund's discount would narrow within six months.
The buyback-at-cost promise is a prohibited guarantee against loss, even though the shares rose.
Only a written, signed guarantee is prohibited; a spoken promise to repurchase the shares at the customer's cost is not.

explanation: NASAA prohibits a broker-dealer or its agent from guaranteeing a customer against loss in a securities account or securities transaction. Promising that the firm will repurchase the shares at the customer's cost is that guarantee. The violation is making the promise, so a later gain and the lack of firm approval do not make it lawful. A closed-end fund has no standing duty to redeem at the buyer's cost, and this promise is not the same as accurately describing a security that carries a third-party guarantee.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the lack of a payout as a defense. The prohibited act is making the guarantee, not later handing the customer money.
distractorExplanations.b: Recasts a promise to repurchase at the customer's cost as a market opinion. A cost-based buyback is a guarantee against loss.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a writing requirement the policy does not impose. A spoken promise to repurchase shares at the customer's cost is still a guarantee against loss.

prompt: A customer asks her agent to keep her $8,400 proceeds check, payable to her, in his desk drawer for three weeks while she travels, instead of sending the funds through the broker-dealer. The agent agrees and does not put the check in his own bank. Under NASAA's policy for agents, which statement is correct?

options.text: The arrangement is allowed because the customer asked for it and the agent will not deposit the $8,400 check in his personal bank.
The agent may keep the check if a supervisor initials the envelope when the customer comes back from the trip.
The custody ban binds the broker-dealer only, so the agent may keep the customer's unendorsed check in his desk.
The agent may not keep the check; an agent is prohibited from acting as custodian for a customer's money.

explanation: NASAA's dishonest-practices policy for agents prohibits an agent from acting as a custodian for a customer's money. Agreeing to keep the customer's $8,400 proceeds check in a desk drawer is custody of client funds, even though the agent never deposits the check in a personal bank account. Those funds belong in the broker-dealer's handling of the account, not in the agent's own safekeeping.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses this hold with a personal-bank deposit. The ban on acting as custodian applies even when the $8,400 check is never deposited in the agent's bank.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats a later supervisor's initials as permission. An agent may not agree to custody of customer money and cure it with a signature after the trip.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats custody as a firm-only rule. NASAA also prohibits the agent from acting as custodian for the customer's money, even when the check is unendorsed.

prompt: Mid-morning, a customer's adult son phones the agent and says his mother wants her utility shares sold today. No one has authorized the son to direct the account, and the customer has not called. What should the agent do with that request?

options.text: Decline the request. A sale on the son's call would be a transaction without the customer's authorization.
Enter the sale, because an adult child may direct a parent's brokerage account for a single security on a single day without a form.
Enter the sale if the son promises that his mother will sign an authorization letter within ten business days after the trade.
Enter the sale as a discretionary order, since the agent can choose the time of execution and the customer already owns the shares.

explanation: NASAA prohibits executing a transaction for a customer without authorization. A family relationship does not give the son power to direct the account, so selling on his call would be an unauthorized transaction. The agent should decline and take instructions from the customer, or from someone she has actually authorized. Authority to pick the time of a sale she never ordered does not create the missing permission.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats a family relationship as trading authority. An adult child cannot direct a parent's account for a day without the customer's authorization.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a ten-day paperwork window. The son cannot sell first and have his mother sign an authorization after the trade.
distractorExplanations.d: Misapplies time-and-price discretion. Choosing when to execute does not authorize a sale the customer never approved.

prompt: An agent recommends stock of Pinnacle Tools. Pinnacle's parent owns Pinnacle and also owns a controlling block of the agent's broker-dealer. The agent describes the business accurately and never mentions that link. What does NASAA require before the sale?

options.text: Nothing further is required, because an accurate description of Pinnacle's business removes any duty to mention the parent's ownership of the firm.
Disclose the common-control relationship before the sale, and provide written disclosure by completion of the trade.
Disclose the relationship only if Pinnacle falls in price and the customer then files a complaint about the recommendation.
Refuse the order. A broker-dealer may not sell the stock of a company with which it is under common control.

explanation: When a broker-dealer is under common control with the issuer, NASAA requires disclosure of that control to the customer before the firm enters the purchase or sale. If the first disclosure is oral, written disclosure must follow at or before completion of the transaction. An accurate description of the business does not replace that disclosure, and common control does not ban the sale.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a fair business description as a substitute for conflict disclosure. The common-control relationship still has to be disclosed to the customer.
distractorExplanations.c: Delays disclosure until a loss and a complaint. NASAA requires the control disclosure before the transaction, not after a decline.
distractorExplanations.d: Overstates the rule into a ban. Securities of a commonly controlled issuer may be sold if the relationship is disclosed as required.

prompt: From inventory, a dealer sells an actively traded common stock to a customer at a price 9% above the contemporaneous market. A compliance officer says this is proper because the firm's manual allows any markup under 10%. How does NASAA judge that reasoning?

options.text: The officer is right. NASAA treats any inventory markup under 10% on a common stock as reasonably related to the current market price.
The fill is proper whenever the confirmation states that the firm acted as principal, no matter how far the 9% price is from the market.
The 10% manual is not the test. This 9% price still has to be reasonably related to the current market.
Judge the markup against the firm's average commission on agency trades that day, not against the stock's market price.

explanation: NASAA prohibits a transaction at a price not reasonably related to the current market price of the security. On an actively traded stock, a markup of 9% is measured against that market. A firm manual that allows any markup under 10% does not create a safe harbor and does not make this price compliant. Stating on the confirmation that the firm acted as principal does not cure an unreasonable price.

distractorExplanations.a: Invents a 10% safe harbor. NASAA's test is whether the 9% price is reasonably related to the current market, and a house manual cannot create a percentage shelter.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses principal-capacity disclosure with price fairness. A confirmation showing a principal trade does not make a 9% markup reasonable.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses the wrong benchmark. The comparison is to the stock's current market price, not to that day's average agency commission.

prompt: Months after buying one growth fund, a customer is urged by the agent to redeem it and buy a nearly identical growth fund at another sponsor. The switch would impose a new sales charge, and the only reason given is a fresh start. What is the problem under NASAA's investment-company policy?

options.text: There is no problem. A new sales charge is simply the ordinary cost of moving a customer from one fund sponsor to another sponsor.
The only possible problem is a missed quantity discount, and nothing in these facts shows a sale made just below a breakpoint.
Several months of ownership cure the switch, so the new sales charge is allowed once the customer has held the first fund that long.
The switch into a similar fund lacks reasonable grounds and imposes a new sales charge without a real benefit to the customer.

explanation: NASAA's investment-company policy treats it as a dishonest practice to recommend redeeming fund shares in order to buy a different portfolio with similar objectives, unless there are reasonable grounds to believe the switch suits the customer in light of the customer's situation, other holdings, and the transaction charges. A fresh start is not those grounds, and the new sales charge is a cost without a corresponding benefit.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores the similar-fund switch. A new sales charge is not automatically suitable just because the customer is changing sponsors.
distractorExplanations.b: Mislabels the conduct as a breakpoint problem. These facts are a redemption into a similar fund, not a sale placed just below a discount level.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a holding-period cure. Months in the first fund do not make a similar-fund switch suitable when it adds a sales charge for a fresh start.

prompt: A brochure describes a mutual fund as no-load. The fund has no front-end sales charge and no contingent deferred sales charge, but it deducts a 12b-1 fee of 0.75% of average net assets each year. Under NASAA's investment-company policy, may the brochure say no-load?

options.text: No. The 0.75% 12b-1 fee exceeds the 0.25% ceiling for a no-load label.
Yes. No-load means only that the buyer pays nothing on the day of purchase, so a 12b-1 fee of any size is compatible with that label.
Yes, if the brochure also prints the ticker symbol and the principal underwriter's name somewhere in the text.
Yes, if a footnote states the 0.75% 12b-1 fee, because disclosing the fee permits the no-load label at any level.

explanation: NASAA's investment-company policy bars calling shares no-load when a Rule 12b-1 fee, alone or with a service fee, exceeds 0.25% of average net fund assets per year. This fund's 0.75% 12b-1 fee is over that line, so the no-load claim is a misleading sales statement even though the buyer pays no front-end load and no contingent deferred sales charge. A footnote that prints the fee does not restore the label.

distractorExplanations.b: Defines no-load as the absence of a charge on purchase day only. A 12b-1 fee of 0.75% exceeds the 0.25% limit and blocks the no-load label.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a ticker and an underwriter's name as a cure. Those details do not make a fund with a 0.75% 12b-1 fee a no-load fund.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats disclosure as permission. Printing the 0.75% fee in a footnote does not allow a no-load claim once the fee exceeds 0.25%.

prompt: After an opening purchase on margin, the firm mails a margin agreement. The trade settles, and months pass with no signature and no follow-up. Which statement matches NASAA's rule on margin accounts?

options.text: The account complies. Once a margin trade settles, the margin agreement is optional unless the customer asks to withdraw the shares.
A signed margin agreement was due promptly after that first margin trade, and leaving it unsigned for months fails the rule.
The missing paper is the loan-consent form, and without it a margin purchase may not remain open after settlement.
The firm had to have the signed margin agreement in hand before it could accept the customer's first margin order.

explanation: NASAA prohibits transactions in a margin account unless the firm obtains a properly executed written margin agreement promptly after the initial transaction in that account. The agreement need not be signed before the first order, but leaving it unsigned for months after settlement is not prompt. Permission to lend the customer's securities is a different form, and the customer does not have to sign that form to keep the margin position.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the margin agreement as optional after settlement. NASAA requires a signed agreement promptly after the first margin transaction.
distractorExplanations.c: Names the wrong form. Consent to lend securities is not required to keep a margin purchase open; the missing document is the margin agreement.
distractorExplanations.d: Moves the deadline too early. The agreement is due promptly after the initial margin trade, not before the firm may accept that first order.

prompt: Fully paid customer shares are pledged, together with other securities, to a bank loan that finances the broker-dealer's own operating expenses. The customers owe the firm nothing on those shares and never consented in writing. Which NASAA violation is this?

options.text: A permitted financing step. A broker-dealer may pledge any customer shares it holds to fund its own operating expenses without asking the customers.
A problem only if the bank loan is still outstanding after a full calendar quarter, and not before that time has run.
A prohibited hypothecation of fully paid customer securities on which the firm has no lien and no written consent.
Ordinary rehypothecation, which may reach the full market value of every customer account, including accounts with no debit.

explanation: NASAA prohibits hypothecating a customer's securities when the firm has no lien on them, unless the customer gives written consent, and it separately requires free securities to be segregated. Fully paid shares are not collateral for the customer's own debit, because there is none. Pledging them, without written consent, to secure a bank loan for the firm's operating expenses is a prohibited hypothecation.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats fully paid customer shares as firm property. Those shares may not be pledged to fund the broker-dealer's own expenses without a lien and written consent.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents a one-quarter timer. The violation is the pledge of fully paid securities itself, and it does not wait for a calendar quarter to pass.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses this pledge with rehypothecation of a customer's margin debit. Fully paid shares, in accounts with no debit, are not collateral up to account value.

prompt: During a popular new-issue distribution, a broker-dealer places most of its allotment in officers' personal accounts and the firm's trading account. Public customers who had asked for shares receive none. Which duty has the firm missed?

options.text: No duty was missed. When public demand exceeds the allotment, the firm may keep the shares for its officers and its own trading account.
The registration duty. Shares moved into officers' personal accounts become unregistered the moment they leave the selling allotment.
The custody duty. Parking new-issue shares in employee and proprietary accounts means the firm has taken custody of client funds.
The duty to make a bona fide public offering of the shares allotted to the firm.

explanation: NASAA requires a broker-dealer that receives securities for distribution to make a bona fide public offering of all the shares allotted to it. Putting most of a popular new issue into officers' accounts and the firm's trading account, while public customers who asked for shares receive none, withholds the offering from the public. That failure is separate from whether the issue itself was registered.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the duty. Keeping the allotment for officers and the firm's account, while public customers who asked receive nothing, is not a bona fide public offering.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses registration status with distribution conduct. The shares do not become unregistered because officers receive them, but the public-offering duty is still missed.
distractorExplanations.c: Misapplies custody. Placing new-issue shares in proprietary and employee accounts is a distribution failure, not custody of client funds.

prompt: In a micro-cap with one dealer, the broker-dealer's own bid and offer are the only active quotations, and the firm holds most of the float. An agent tells a retail buyer the stock is being offered at the market. What is wrong with that phrase?

options.text: The firm may not call the price at the market when no market exists apart from the one the firm controls.
Nothing is wrong. A broker-dealer's own bid and offer are the market whenever the firm will trade with a retail buyer at those prices.
The phrase is improper only when the confirmation labels the firm's spread as a commission instead of a principal markup.
The at-the-market ban applies only in a distribution, so a dominated micro-cap may be described that way in secondary trading.

explanation: NASAA prohibits representing that a security is offered at the market, or at a price related to the market, unless the broker-dealer knows or has reasonable grounds to believe that a market exists other than one the firm made, created, or controls. Here the firm's quotations are the only active market and the firm holds most of the float, so the at-the-market claim is misleading. The agent may describe the firm's own bid and offer as the firm's price.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats the firm's own quote as an independent market. NASAA bars an at-the-market claim when no market exists apart from the one the firm controls.
distractorExplanations.c: Focuses on confirmation wording. The violation is the at-the-market representation itself, not whether the spread is labeled a commission.
distractorExplanations.d: Limits the ban to distributions. NASAA also bars an at-the-market claim in secondary trading when no market exists apart from the firm.

prompt: Selling a new mutual fund's shares, an agent tells the buyer the prospectus is optional reading. On the confirmation's due date the customer still has no prospectus. Under NASAA's dishonest-practices policy, what was required?

options.text: Nothing more was required. For this mutual fund the prospectus is optional reading, and the confirmation alone finishes the firm's disclosure.
Furnish a prospectus no later than the due date of the confirmation.
Furnish a prospectus only if the customer requests it in writing within five business days after the confirmation.
Furnish a prospectus before the buyer's check clears, and only when the fund charges a front-end sales load.

explanation: NASAA requires a broker-dealer selling securities in an offering to furnish the customer a prospectus no later than the due date of the confirmation. Telling the buyer the prospectus is optional, and failing to deliver it by that due date, violates the rule. The duty does not depend on a written request from the customer or on whether the fund charges a front-end sales load.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the prospectus as optional. In this offering the customer must receive it no later than the confirmation's due date.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds a written-request condition the rule does not contain. Delivery is required by the confirmation's due date whether or not the customer asks.
