sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go item (Tier A bank expansion 2026-10-15).

prompt: A state-registered adviser pays a current client to record a short video praising the firm's retirement planning, then posts the video on its public website with no statement that she is a client or that she was paid. Under NASAA's model advertising rule, which statement is correct?

options.text: It may stay up only with clear and prominent disclosure of her client status, the payment, and the conflict, plus the compensation terms and a written agreement.
It is forbidden in every case, so the firm must remove it even after adding a caption that names her as a client, states the payment, and describes the conflict the payment creates.
It is allowed as posted, because a current client's sincere praise is not an advertisement.
It is allowed once she adds that past results do not guarantee future results.

explanation: NASAA's model rule treats a statement by a current client as a testimonial. When the adviser pays for it, the advertisement must clearly and prominently disclose that the speaker is a client, that compensation was provided, and the material conflict the payment creates, and it must disclose the material terms of that compensation. The adviser must also have a written agreement describing the agreed activity and the terms of the compensation. A bare video of praise hides that the client was paid to speak.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats every testimonial as banned. The amended rule allows a paid client statement when client status, the compensation and its terms, the conflict, and a written agreement are all in place.
distractorExplanations.c: Mistakes a public testimonial for a private remark. A website video of praise aimed at prospects is an advertisement and must meet the testimonial conditions.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes a results disclaimer for the required facts. That legend does not disclose that the speaker is a paid client or supply the written agreement.

prompt: A state-registered adviser's brochure claims clients earned more than the broad market last year. The brochure omits any basis for that performance claim: it names no accounts, no fee treatment, and no calculation the firm could show the Administrator. How does NASAA's advertising rule treat the claim?

options.text: The claim is acceptable if the brochure adds that past performance does not guarantee future results and that markets can fall as well as rise over any period a reader might care about.
The claim is improper, because the adviser has no reasonable basis it could substantiate on demand.
The claim is acceptable, because beating the market is a slogan rather than a statement of fact.
The claim may be used only after the Administrator approves the wording in writing.

explanation: NASAA's advertising rule bars a material statement of fact when the adviser lacks a reasonable basis for believing it can substantiate the statement if the Administrator demands support. A performance claim that omits any basis, with no accounts, fee treatment, or calculation behind it, fails that test. A future-results legend does not create the missing support, and the Administrator does not pre-clear the sentence.

distractorExplanations.a: Relies on a disclaimer to cure a claim the firm cannot support. The rule requires a basis the adviser can substantiate, not a warning that results may change.
distractorExplanations.c: Mislabels a comparative performance assertion as puffery. Saying clients earned more than the market is a material statement of fact and needs a basis.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents an approval step. The Administrator does not pre-clear the wording; the adviser must be able to substantiate the claim on demand.

prompt: While reviewing a mutual fund with a new customer, an agent marks the prospectus with a highlighter on the objective and the fee table, then says those marked passages are all the customer needs to read. Under NASAA's statement of policy on dishonest practices of broker-dealers and agents, what is the result?

options.text: Permitted, because marking the objective and the fee table helps the customer focus on cost and strategy instead of hunting for those facts in a long disclosure document.
Permitted, because the customer still received every page of the prospectus.
Prohibited, because the highlighting and the claim that those passages are all the customer must read are meant to defeat the prospectus.
Permitted if the agent also offers to read the unmarked pages aloud on request.

explanation: NASAA's statement of policy on dishonest or unethical practices of broker-dealers and agents treats as deceptive a sales presentation designed to supplement, detract from, supersede, or defeat a prospectus or other disclosure. Highlighting the objective and the fee table, then telling the customer those passages are all that must be read, is meant to defeat the rest of the document. Helpful intent and delivery of every page do not make that presentation lawful.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats helpful intent as a defense. Steering the customer to a few marked passages, and away from the rest of the prospectus, is a presentation designed to defeat that disclosure.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses delivery of the full prospectus with a lawful presentation. Handing over every page does not authorize telling the customer that the unmarked disclosure can be skipped.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds an oral offer the rule does not treat as a cure. The violation is a presentation meant to defeat the prospectus, and offering to read the rest later does not undo that instruction.

prompt: While a new bond issue is in registration, a syndicate member prepares a boxed notice for the newspaper. Which item may the notice include under the limits on tombstone advertising?

options.text: A recommendation that conservative investors buy the bonds, plus each syndicate member's percentage participation and the net proceeds after the spread.
The net proceeds the issuer will receive after the underwriting spread.
A projection of the price at which the bonds should trade after issuance.
Where a reader can obtain a prospectus.

explanation: A tombstone during registration is a notice, not a sales piece. It may identify the issuer and the security and tell readers where to obtain a prospectus. It may not recommend the bonds, project how they will trade, state net proceeds after the underwriting spread, or list each member's participation. Those additions would turn the notice into a sales communication.

distractorExplanations.a: Packs a recommendation, each member's participation, and net proceeds into the notice. All three sit outside what a tombstone may say, and a recommendation is a sales pitch.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses gross proceeds, which a tombstone may state, with net proceeds after the spread, which the notice may not state.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds a price projection. A tombstone may not predict how the security will trade or use language meant to build enthusiasm for the issue.

prompt: Northline Advisors, registered with the state, places this footnote under a table of client returns: the Administrator has reviewed and approved the way these returns were calculated. What is the status of that footnote?

options.text: Prohibited. The firm may not imply the Administrator approved the calculation.
Permitted, because state registration already means the Administrator has reviewed the firm's advertising and signed off on how client returns are presented to the public.
Permitted if the footnote is printed in type smaller than the return table.
Permitted for a state-registered adviser, but not for a federal covered adviser.

explanation: NASAA's advertising rule forbids an adviser to state or imply that the Administrator approved or reviewed the calculation or presentation of performance. Registration is not an endorsement of the firm's numbers. Type size, and whether the adviser is state-registered or federal covered, does not create permission to claim that approval.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses registration with approval of a performance calculation. An effective registration does not mean the Administrator reviewed or blessed the return methodology.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats smaller type as a cure. The violation is the claim of regulatory approval, and shrinking the footnote does not remove that claim.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a split the rule does not draw. Implying that the Administrator approved the performance presentation is prohibited for this state-registered adviser.

prompt: In a magazine advertisement, Pine Counsel shows its growth composite's gross return in large type and leaves the net return out of the page entirely. Under NASAA's performance rules, what must the firm do?

options.text: Leave the page as it is, provided a nearby sentence says advisory fees differ from client to client and that the gross figure is shown before those fees are taken out.
Show net performance at least as prominently, for the same period and the same methodology.
Omit net results whenever every person who will see the page is already a client.
Replace the missing net figure with a statement that the Administrator reviewed the gross return.

explanation: When an adviser advertises gross performance, NASAA's rule requires net performance as well, calculated over the same period and with the same type of return and methodology, and shown at least as prominently as the gross figure. Dropping the net result, or burying the effect of fees in a general sentence, presents the return before the cost of advice and overstates what a client kept.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a fee disclaimer as a substitute for net performance. The rule requires the net figure itself, at equal prominence, not a sentence saying that fees vary.
distractorExplanations.c: Limits the duty to prospects. The gross-and-net requirement applies to the performance presentation and is not waived because the readers are already clients.
distractorExplanations.d: Invokes Administrator review, which the adviser may not claim, and still fails to show net performance beside the gross return.

prompt: A flyer from an investment adviser representative describes the income and growth a retiree might receive from the firm's strategy and says nothing about the strategy's risks or limits. What is the problem under NASAA's advertising rule?

options.text: There is no problem, because a flyer may describe possible income and growth so long as it does not name a specific security or promise that every retiree will receive the same cash flow.
There is a problem only if a reader later loses money on the strategy.
Benefits are discussed with no fair and balanced treatment of the material risks.
The flyer needed each reader's signed acknowledgment before it could be handed out.

explanation: NASAA's advertising rule does not let an adviser discuss potential benefits of its services or methods without fair and balanced treatment of the material risks and limitations that go with those benefits. A flyer that describes income and growth and is silent on risk fails that standard. The violation is in the communication itself and does not depend on a later loss or on a signed acknowledgment.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the absence of a named security or a hard promise as permission to discuss benefits alone. The rule still requires fair and balanced treatment of the material risks and limits.
distractorExplanations.b: Makes the violation depend on a client loss. The unfair presentation is improper when it is distributed, whether or not anyone later loses money.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a signed-acknowledgment condition. The rule requires balanced disclosure in the flyer, not a signature from each reader.

prompt: Cedar Wealth pays a magazine to survey planners and then cites the resulting top-planner badge in its advertisement. The survey made favorable answers easy to give and unfavorable answers hard, and the ad names neither the magazine nor the payment. What does NASAA require?

options.text: Keep the badge, because any ranking a magazine publishes may be quoted without asking how the questionnaire was built or whether the adviser paid for the placement.
Keep the badge if at least half the planners surveyed were already clients of Cedar Wealth.
Keep the badge only if a state Administrator or an exchange ran the survey.
Drop the badge unless the survey was fair and the ad or the rating discloses the rater, the date, the period, and any pay.

explanation: Before an adviser uses a third-party rating, it must have a reasonable basis to believe the questionnaire made favorable and unfavorable responses equally easy and was not designed to produce a predetermined result. The advertisement must also disclose, or the adviser must reasonably believe the rating discloses, the date and the period, who created the rating, and any compensation paid to obtain or use it. A survey built to draw praise, with the payment hidden, fails both parts.

distractorExplanations.a: Assumes a magazine label makes the rating usable. The adviser must still believe the survey was fair, and the ad or the rating must disclose the rater, the date, the period, and any pay.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents a client-participation quota. The rule looks at whether favorable and unfavorable answers were equally easy, not at what share of respondents were clients.
distractorExplanations.c: Requires a regulator or an exchange to run the survey. A private rater may be cited when the survey design and the disclosures meet the rule.

prompt: Someone who has never been a client writes a glowing online review of a state-registered adviser, and the adviser gives that person a gift card for the review. How does NASAA's advertising rule classify the review?

options.text: As an endorsement, because the writer is not a current client.
As a testimonial, because the gift card is compensation and any paid statement praising the adviser's services is a testimonial no matter who wrote it.
As a third-party rating, because an outsider posted it on the internet.
As outside the rule, because the writer is not a registered person.

explanation: Under NASAA's definitions, a testimonial is a statement by a current client or investor, and an endorsement is a statement by someone else that approves of the adviser, describes an experience, or refers people to the firm. Paying for the review does not change that line, and one person's compensated review is not a third-party rating prepared in the ordinary course of a rating business. The endorsement conditions, including disclosure of the compensation, still apply.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses payment with the definition. Compensation does not turn a non-client's statement into a testimonial; a testimonial must come from a current client or investor.
distractorExplanations.c: Mislabels a single paid review as a third-party rating. A rating is a score prepared by an unrelated person in the ordinary course, not one review bought with a gift card.
distractorExplanations.d: Ties the rule to the writer's registration. Endorsements cover statements by people who are not clients, whether or not those people are registered.

prompt: Without being asked, a state-registered adviser mails one prospect a letter offering its services and enclosing backtested results for a strategy no real account has ever used. The firm has no policy on who should receive such figures and states no assumptions. How is the letter treated?

options.text: As outside the advertising rule, because a letter to a single prospect is only correspondence, and backtested results are research rather than performance of any kind.
As an advertisement with hypothetical performance that lacks the required safeguards.
As permitted, because the prospect can ignore the enclosure if the assumptions are unclear.
As permitted only after the Administrator approves the backtest in writing.

explanation: Backtested results are hypothetical performance, because no portfolio of the adviser actually achieved them. A communication that offers advisory services and includes hypothetical performance is an advertisement even when it goes to one person, unless it answers an unsolicited request or is a one-on-one communication to a private-fund investor. Here the adviser mailed a prospect first. Hypothetical performance may be used only under policies designed to keep it relevant to the audience, and only if the criteria, assumptions, risks, and limitations are explained. This letter has none of that.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses the one-recipient idea and mislabels a backtest as research. Hypothetical performance pulls even a single-person sales letter into the definition of an advertisement.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaves compliance to the reader. The adviser must adopt the policies and explain the assumptions before using the backtest, not rely on the prospect to set the letter aside.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a pre-approval by the Administrator. The conditions are the adviser's policies and the disclosures about the figures, not a regulatory sign-off.

prompt: A quarterly mailer from a state-registered adviser shows the results of only the three holdings that rose the most inside one client portfolio and does not mention the rest of that portfolio. What does the model rule require for this extracted performance?

options.text: Obtain that client's written consent and add a broad market index for the same span, which together replace any need to show how the rest of the portfolio actually performed.
Nothing further, because each of those rising results is accurate on its own.
Provide, or promptly offer, the performance of the whole portfolio those holdings came from.
Submit the extracted figures to the Administrator before the mailer is used.

explanation: Extracted performance is the result of a subset of investments taken from a portfolio. NASAA's rule bars showing that subset unless the advertisement also provides, or offers to provide promptly, the performance of the total portfolio, so a reader can see what the selected holdings left out. Client consent, a market index, or Administrator approval is not the requirement, and the adviser may not claim the Administrator reviewed the figures.

distractorExplanations.a: Substitutes client consent and an index for the portfolio the holdings were taken from. The rule requires the total portfolio's results, or a prompt offer of them.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats accurate pieces as a fair presentation. True figures for the winners still mislead when the rest of the portfolio is omitted and not offered.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a filing with the Administrator. Extracted performance is cured by showing or offering the whole portfolio, not by regulatory pre-clearance.

prompt: At a seminar, a broker-dealer hands prospects a one-page sheet that retells only the issuer's growth story and says they can skip the prospectus because the sheet is the version that matters. Under NASAA's rule on broker-dealer advertising, what is the result?

options.text: Lawful, because prospects can still request the prospectus later, and a short sheet is allowed when it uses the issuer's own growth story and adds no independent price target.
Lawful, because the sheet contains no false number and agents are not fiduciaries on every sale.
Lawful if the seminar is held only for people who already own the security.
Unlawful, because the sheet is designed to supersede the prospectus.

explanation: NASAA treats as deceptive any advertising or sales presentation designed to supplement, detract from, supersede, or defeat the purpose of a prospectus or other required disclosure. A sheet that tells prospects to skip the prospectus and rely on a growth story does exactly that. Offering the prospectus on request, and the absence of a made-up number, does not repair a presentation built to replace the disclosure document.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats later access to the prospectus as a cure. The violation is a sales piece written to take the place of the prospectus, not the lack of a price target.
distractorExplanations.b: Stops at the absence of a false numeral and at fiduciary status. A presentation can mislead by pushing readers past the prospectus even when every sentence is literally true.
distractorExplanations.c: Limits the rule to people who do not yet own the security. The ban on a sales presentation that defeats the prospectus applies to the communication itself.

prompt: Harbor Advisors, state-registered, wants to advertise a composite that is too new to have a five-year record or a ten-year record. Which presentation meets NASAA's performance rule?

options.text: Whichever periods the firm prefers, as long as a footnote says the composite is new and warns that past results may not be repeated for every reader of the advertisement.
A projection filling the five-year and ten-year columns so the table looks as complete as an older composite.
No performance at all, because a composite without a ten-year record may not show returns.
The one-year result, with the composite's life replacing the missing longer periods, at equal prominence.

explanation: For a portfolio other than a private fund, NASAA requires one-year, five-year, and ten-year results, each with equal prominence, ending no earlier than the most recent calendar year-end. When the composite has not existed for a prescribed period, the life of the composite is substituted for that period. A firm-chosen set of periods, or a projection used to fill empty columns, does not satisfy the rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Lets the firm pick periods and rely on a footnote. The rule fixes the periods and requires equal prominence, and a new-composite warning does not replace a missing prescribed period.
distractorExplanations.b: Fills the gap with a projection. A projected result is hypothetical performance, not a substitute for the life of the composite in the prescribed-period table.
distractorExplanations.c: Bars performance advertising until a ten-year record exists. A newer composite may be shown by using its full life in place of each period it has not been around for.

prompt: After dinner, an investment adviser representative posts on a personal social-media account that anyone can open. The post urges followers to hire the representative to manage their stocks and to buy a listed common stock the representative names. The firm's name does not appear. Under NASAA rules, how is that post treated?

options.text: As an advertisement that the firm must supervise and keep
As a private remark outside NASAA rules, because the account is personal and the firm's name is absent
As a separate message to each follower who sees it, and therefore not an advertisement
As permitted market commentary unless the issuer of that stock paid the representative to publish it

explanation: Under NASAA rules, a communication to more than one person that offers an investment adviser's securities advisory services to prospective clients is an advertisement. This post does that, and it also tells followers to buy a named stock. Putting the post on a personal account, or leaving the firm's name off it, does not take the communication outside the rule. The firm must supervise the post and keep a copy, and the post must not be misleading.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats a personal label as an exemption. A public post that solicits followers to hire the representative and buy a stock is still an advertisement the firm must supervise and keep.
distractorExplanations.c: Splits one public post into private messages. A single post shown to followers is a communication to more than one person, so it is an advertisement.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a payment test. The post is an advertisement because it offers advisory services and names a stock, whether or not the issuer paid for it.

prompt: Midweek, a state-registered adviser emails one current client a bond recommendation for that client's existing account. The same week, the adviser emails a brochure to a wide group of prospects inviting them to hire the adviser to manage their securities. Under NASAA rules, which statement is accurate?

options.text: Both emails are advertisements, because each one discusses securities or the adviser's work
The client email is not an advertisement; the prospect brochure is an advertisement
Neither email is an advertisement, because the client already has an account and the brochure names no particular bond
The client email is the advertisement because it names a bond, and the brochure is not because it only describes the service

explanation: A written recommendation sent to a single current client about that client's existing account is not an advertisement under NASAA rules. It is still a required record, and it must not mislead. An email to a wide group of prospects that invites them to hire the adviser to manage their securities is a communication to more than one person offering advisory services, so it is an advertisement and must be kept as one.

distractorExplanations.a: Collapses the two emails into one category. Discussing securities does not make a one-client recommendation an advertisement.
distractorExplanations.c: Misses the prospect mailing. An invitation to a wide group of prospects to hire the adviser is an advertisement even when no particular bond is named.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the test. Naming a bond in a note to one client does not create an advertisement, and an offer of the advisory service to many prospects is an advertisement.

prompt: Sorting the week's files, a state-registered adviser decides what to retain after emailing one client a securities recommendation. Under the NASAA recordkeeping rule, which item must the adviser keep?

options.text: Every message the representative sent that day, including notes that never mention a security or a client
A newspaper story about the issuer that the adviser did not write and did not send to anyone
The email that set out the recommendation to the client
A later summary the representative composes from memory if the original email is deleted

explanation: The NASAA recordkeeping rule requires an investment adviser to keep written communications it sends that contain a recommendation or advice. The email is that record. A note that never mentions a security or a client is not a communication the rule requires. An unsolicited newspaper story the adviser did not prepare and did not circulate is not a communication the adviser must keep. A summary written from memory does not replace the email that was sent.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats every outgoing message as a required record. The rule keeps a communication that contains a recommendation, not a note that never mentions a security or a client.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats an outside article as the adviser's communication. The rule does not require keeping a market story the adviser neither prepared nor circulated.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes a recollection for the record. The duty is to keep the recommendation that was sent, not a summary written after the email is gone.

prompt: While scrolling a public feed, an agent shares a stranger's post that urges readers to buy a thinly traded stock, and adds that this is the one to buy. Under NASAA rules, what has the agent done?

options.text: Nothing that NASAA rules address, because a stranger wrote the original sentences
Opened a private conversation with the stranger, which those rules do not cover
Stayed in compliance, because the stranger, rather than the agent, remains the author of the claim
Adopted the urging as the agent's own recommendation

explanation: When an agent republishes a third-party post about a security and tells followers to buy that stock, the agent adopts the recommendation. It is then the agent's own communication to the public. The communication must not be misleading, and the broker-dealer must be able to keep it. The agent cannot leave responsibility with the stranger after endorsing the post.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at who typed the original sentences. Sharing the post and telling followers to buy adopts the urging as the agent's recommendation.
distractorExplanations.b: Misreads a public share as a private chat. The endorsement is visible to the feed, so it is not a conversation with the stranger alone.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaves the claim with the stranger after the agent has endorsed it. Adoption makes the recommendation the agent's own communication.

prompt: From a personal social-media profile, an agent tells followers that a new offering is safe because the state Administrator cleared it and stands behind the shares. Registration of the offering is effective. Which later post complies with the Uniform Securities Act?

options.text: One that says the offering is registered and does not claim the Administrator approved it
The original wording, because an effective registration is the Administrator's endorsement of the shares
The original wording, if a follow-up comment tells followers to read the prospectus before they buy
The original wording, if the agent first emails the Administrator and asks permission to describe the clearance

explanation: The Uniform Securities Act forbids representing that the Administrator has approved a security or passed on its merits. An agent may say, if it is true, that an offering is registered. Registration is not a statement that the Administrator stands behind the shares. A prospectus reminder or a request for permission does not make an approval claim lawful. The same limit applies on a personal social-media profile.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses effectiveness with approval. Registration means filing requirements were met, not that the Administrator endorsed the shares.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a prospectus reminder as a cure. The violation is the claim that the Administrator stands behind the offering.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a permission process. The Administrator cannot authorize an agent to imply that the office approved the security.

prompt: In a private note addressed only to one long-time client, an adviser recommends a corporate bond and praises its coupon, but leaves out a default the issuer disclosed that week. The note goes to nobody else. Under the Uniform Securities Act, which statement is true?

options.text: The omission is acceptable, because a note to a single client is not an advertisement and disclosure rules stop there
The omission is unlawful even though the note is not an advertisement
The omission is acceptable, because the client could have found the default in the issuer's public filing
The omission is acceptable, because the coupon the adviser praises is the coupon the bond actually pays

explanation: Antifraud provisions apply to a recommendation made to a single client. Praising the coupon while leaving out a current default omits a material fact needed to keep the recommendation from misleading the client. The note is not an advertisement, because it is addressed to one person, but that label does not excuse the omission. A correct coupon figure does not fill the gap.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the advertisement definition with antifraud. A one-client note is not an advertisement, and it still may not omit a material fact.
distractorExplanations.c: Shifts the adviser's duty onto the client. The person making the recommendation must not omit a material fact such as a current default.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats one true figure as the whole note. An accurate coupon beside a hidden default is still misleading.

prompt: A portfolio manager at a state-registered adviser writes the memorandum of a client's securities order. The memorandum shows the terms, the account, and that the adviser used discretion. Under the NASAA recordkeeping rule, what must happen to that memorandum?

options.text: It may be discarded once the trade confirmation is sent, because the confirmation replaces it
It must be filed with the Administrator before the order is routed to the broker-dealer
The adviser must keep it as a required record of the order
It may be discarded, because the power of attorney already documents a discretionary order

explanation: The NASAA recordkeeping rule requires an investment adviser to keep a memorandum of each order it gives for the purchase or sale of a security. The memorandum must show the terms and the account, and an order entered under discretion must be designated as discretionary. A trade confirmation does not replace that memorandum. The rule does not require the memorandum to be filed with the Administrator before the order is routed, and a power of attorney does not take its place.

distractorExplanations.a: Substitutes the confirmation for the order memorandum. The adviser must keep the memorandum even after the confirmation is sent.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents a pre-order filing. The Administrator may examine the memorandum, but the rule does not require filing it before the order is routed.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the power of attorney as a substitute. Discretionary orders are still recorded on an order memorandum, which the adviser must keep.

prompt: A registered agent keeps a public profile of general comments on the firm's services. It names the broker-dealer, which reviewed, approved, and authorized it, and the agent stays within that authority. It limits business to states where the agent is registered or exempt, bars individualized advice and trades elsewhere, and a procedure blocks follow-up. The agent answers no question about a particular security. People in states where the agent is unregistered can see it. Under NASAA internet guidance, what follows?

options.text: The agent must register in every state where a person is able to open the profile and read those comments
The profile is an offer of securities in each viewing state because anyone there can open the page
The agent must remove the profile until every state where it can be seen has granted a registration
Display of that profile is not, by itself, business where the agent is unregistered

explanation: NASAA's interpretive order on internet communications says a general profile is not, by itself, transacting business where the agent is unregistered when its conditions are met. This profile names the broker-dealer, which reviewed, approved, and authorized it, and the agent stays within that authority. It limits business to states where the agent is registered or exempt, bars individualized advice and trades elsewhere, and a procedure blocks that follow-up. The agent does not answer a question about a particular security. Viewers in other states do not, by themselves, create a registration there.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats mere visibility as doing business. NASAA does not require a new registration in every state where someone can open a profile that meets the internet-communications conditions.
distractorExplanations.b: Calls a general, limited profile an offer in each viewing state. Under the order, that profile is not itself a transaction of business there.
distractorExplanations.c: Requires the profile to come down. The order allows a general communication that meets its conditions, including firm approval and no individualized follow-up where the agent is unregistered.

prompt: Addressing clients and prospects together, an agent posts on a personal social-media account that a bond the firm is offering cannot lose money and that the agent will make good any loss in a buyer's account. Under the NASAA statement of policy on dishonest or unethical practices, which statement is accurate?

options.text: The post is an unethical guarantee against loss
The post is allowed because it appears on a personal account rather than on firm letterhead
The post is allowed unless a buyer later loses money and asks the agent to pay
The post is allowed when the bond carries an investment-grade rating from a rating service

explanation: The NASAA statement of policy treats guaranteeing a customer against loss as a dishonest or unethical practice. A post promising that a bond cannot lose money, and that the agent will make good any loss in a buyer's account, is that guarantee. Publishing it on a personal social-media account does not remove it from the policy. The promise is unethical when it is made, and a credit rating does not authorize it.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats the account label as a defense. A guarantee against loss is unethical on a personal social-media account as well as on firm letterhead.
distractorExplanations.c: Postpones the violation until someone demands payment. Making the guarantee is the unethical practice, whether or not a loss has occurred.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses credit quality with a promise of no loss. An investment-grade rating does not permit an agent to guarantee a buyer against loss.

prompt: Posted for the general public, a state-registered adviser's electronic note says only to buy the common stock of a named issuer. The note gives no reason for the recommendation. Under the NASAA recordkeeping rule, what must the adviser keep besides a copy of the note?

options.text: Nothing further, because the note itself is the full record of the recommendation
A memorandum stating the reasons for that recommendation
The street address of every person who might read the public note
A copy of the note stamped by the Administrator before the note is released to the public

Yes, as soon as a resident calls the station to ask for a mailing address, even if the caller accepts nothing
Yes, once the Administrator posts a transcript of the program on the state website for residents to read
No. An out-of-state radio broadcast is not an offer here merely because residents hear it

explanation: An offer is not made in a state merely because residents receive a radio or television program that originates outside the state. This weekly program is produced and broadcast elsewhere, and it is not aimed at a named person here. Hearing it does not, by itself, give this state jurisdiction over that pitch. A letter or email directed to a person in the state and received there would be an offer in the state. A phone call that only asks for an address does not change the broadcast into one.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats every broadcast a resident can hear as a directed offer; the Act excludes an out-of-state radio program that is merely received in the state.
distractorExplanations.b: Turns a request for an address into an offer in the state; asking where to write does not convert an out-of-state broadcast into a directed offer here.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a posting step; whether the broadcast is an offer in the state does not turn on the Administrator putting a transcript on a website.

prompt: During a bond sale, the agent quotes the coupon and the maturity accurately but leaves out a missed payment the agent knew about. The buyer did not know of the miss and still holds the bond. How does the Uniform Securities Act treat that silence?

options.text: As an actionable omission, with the same restorative recovery as a spoken untruth
As harmless, because the coupon and the maturity were correct and leaving a fact out cannot mislead a buyer
As a registration defect only, so the buyer may recover solely if the bond was sold without being registered
As a criminal sentence the Administrator may impose on the agent without taking the case to a court

explanation: Civil liability reaches an omission of a material fact needed to keep what was said from misleading, not only a sentence that is false on its face. A missed payment the agent knew about changes the meaning of a clean coupon-and-maturity pitch, and this buyer did not know of it. The buyer may recover the consideration paid, with interest, costs, and reasonable attorney's fees, less income received, upon tender of the bond. The claim does not depend on a failure to register the bond, and the Administrator does not impose a criminal sentence.

distractorExplanations.b: Limits the claim to words that are false out loud; leaving out a material fact that makes the pitch misleading is the same kind of civil wrong.
distractorExplanations.c: Collapses the omission into a registration defect; the buyer may recover whether or not this bond had to be registered.
distractorExplanations.d: Assigns a criminal sentence to the Administrator; the buyer's remedy for the omission is civil, and a criminal case is brought in court.

prompt: The Administrator is ready to revoke an agent's registration for dishonest sales practices and wants that revocation to be the final order. No hearing has been offered, and no emergency suspension is being used. What must happen first under the Uniform Securities Act?

options.text: Nothing further. A final revocation for dishonest practices may be entered as soon as the staff file is complete
The agent must get notice and a chance for a hearing before the revocation is final
FINRA must adopt the revocation in writing, or the state's order cannot become final
The agent must be offered a chance to pay a money penalty instead of having any hearing

explanation: A final order denying, suspending, or revoking a registration requires prior notice, an opportunity for a hearing, and written findings. The Administrator may not skip the hearing because the staff believes the sales practices were dishonest. An interim postponement or suspension can protect investors while a case is pending, but this matter is not using that interim power and the order sought is a final revocation. A payment does not replace the hearing, and FINRA does not have to adopt the state's order.

distractorExplanations.a: Skips the hearing required before a final revocation; a completed staff file does not replace notice and an opportunity to be heard.
distractorExplanations.c: Hands the last step to FINRA; notice, the hearing, and the final order belong to the Administrator under the Act.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes a penalty payment for the hearing; the Act requires an opportunity to be heard and does not let a payment stand in for it.

prompt: A broker-dealer passed along an issuer's short description that left out a material lawsuit. The firm shows it did not know of the suit and that a careful review of the issuer's public filings would not have revealed it. The buyer did not know either. What is the firm's civil exposure under the Uniform Securities Act?

options.text: Strict liability for the gap, because a firm that forwards an issuer's description answers for every omission no matter what care it used
Liability only if the buyer proves the firm meant to hide the lawsuit from people who bought the security
No liability if the firm proves it did not know and could not reasonably have known
No liability unless the buyer proves the firm skipped reasonable care, because that burden sits with the buyer

explanation: A person who sells a security by means of a material omission is liable unless that person proves both a lack of knowledge and the exercise of reasonable care. This firm did not know of the lawsuit, and a careful review of the public filings would not have shown it, so the defense is met. The buyer does not have to prove that the firm intended to deceive anyone. The buyer also does not carry the burden on reasonable care. That burden is the firm's, and on these facts the firm has carried it.

distractorExplanations.a: Imposes strict liability and erases the care defense; a seller that proves it did not know, and could not reasonably have known, is not liable for that omission.
distractorExplanations.b: Requires the buyer to prove an intent to conceal; civil liability for an omission does not make the buyer prove that the firm meant to hide the fact.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the burden of proof; the seller, not the buyer, must show the lack of knowledge and the exercise of reasonable care.

prompt: After buying shares through an untrue statement she did not know about, a client sold those shares onward and now holds only the cash from that sale. She sues the original seller under the Uniform Securities Act. Which remedy fits her situation?

options.text: No remedy, because a buyer who has sold the shares has given up any civil claim against the original seller
An order that she buy the shares back from the later owner and then tender that new position to the seller
A sum limited to the profit the later buyer earned, which the original seller must equal in full
Damages, reduced by what the shares were worth when she sold them

explanation: A buyer who still owns the security recovers the consideration paid, with interest, costs, and reasonable attorney's fees, less income received, upon tender. This client has sold the shares, so she cannot tender them. She may sue for damages instead. Those damages start from the same restorative amount and subtract the value of the shares when she disposed of them. The claim is not measured by a later buyer's profit, and selling the shares does not erase it.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats continued ownership as a condition of any claim; a buyer who has sold may sue for damages even though she can no longer tender the shares.
distractorExplanations.b: Requires her to reacquire the shares from a later purchaser; the Act lets her recover damages without chasing the certificate she already sold.
distractorExplanations.c: Measures the claim by a later buyer's profit; her damages follow what she paid, reduced by the value when she sold, not by that other person's gain.

prompt: While a revocation proceeding is already underway, the agent files a request to withdraw his registration and asks the Administrator to drop the case. No final order has been entered. What may the Administrator do under the Uniform Securities Act?

options.text: Continue the case and revoke if the grounds are proved
Dismiss the case, because a withdrawal request ends the Administrator's power the day the request is received
Send the case to FINRA, the only forum that can finish a revocation after a withdrawal is requested
Recast the case as a cancellation, the nonpunitive step used when a registrant has died or cannot be found

explanation: A request to withdraw does not shut down a revocation proceeding that has already begun. The Administrator may carry the case through and, with the public interest and a statutory ground shown, revoke the registration. Withdrawal is not cancellation. Cancellation is the nonpunitive step used when a registrant has died, ceased to exist, or cannot be located. The state's proceeding stays with the Administrator rather than moving to FINRA.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats the withdrawal request as an automatic end to a case already underway; the Administrator may continue a pending revocation proceeding.
distractorExplanations.c: Moves a state revocation to FINRA; the proceeding stays with the Administrator, and a withdrawal request does not transfer it.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses revocation with cancellation; asking to withdraw during a disciplinary case is not death, dissolution, or an inability to locate the agent.

prompt: Helen mails her signed acceptance from her home in State B to the agent who mailed her the offering from an office in State A. She had not accepted by phone or in any earlier writing. Under the Uniform Securities Act, where is that acceptance made?

options.text: Only in State B, because she signed at home and the state where the agent receives the form does not count
In State A, where it reached the offeror, with no earlier acceptance outside that state
In neither state, unless she and the agent sign the form together in one room at the same time
In every state the envelope crosses, because each postmark along the route counts as another acceptance

explanation: An offer is accepted in a state when the acceptance is communicated to the offeror in that state and has not previously been communicated to the offeror outside that state. Helen's first acceptance was mailed to the agent in State A. It is an acceptance in State A. Signing at home in State B does not by itself fix the place of acceptance. The two parties need not be in the same room, and states the envelope merely crosses are not separate acceptances.

distractorExplanations.a: Fixes the acceptance at the place of signing and ignores where it was communicated to the offeror, which is the office in State A.
distractorExplanations.c: Requires a face-to-face signing; the Act locates an acceptance by communication to the offeror, including a mailing into the offeror's state.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats each state on the mail route as a new acceptance; the acceptance is made where it is communicated to the offeror in State A.

prompt: Another state's Administrator has revoked this person's agent registration for dishonest practices. This state's Administrator is now reviewing a fresh application, and no separate misconduct has occurred here. What may this Administrator do?

options.text: Nothing yet, because this state must wait for misconduct that occurs inside its own borders
Approve the application, because a revocation entered somewhere else cannot be considered in this state
Deny the application in the public interest, using that other revocation as a ground
Wait for a criminal conviction in the other state, the only outside result this Administrator may rely on

explanation: Being subject to another Administrator's order revoking a registration is a statutory ground for denial. The ground is not limited to a criminal conviction, and it is not limited to misconduct that occurred in this state. Denial still requires a finding that the action is in the public interest. With that finding, this Administrator may deny the new application because of the revocation entered in the other state.

distractorExplanations.a: Limits the grounds to conduct inside this state; another Administrator's revocation is itself a statutory ground that can support a denial here.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats the out-of-state order as irrelevant; that revocation can support denial when this Administrator also finds the action is in the public interest.
distractorExplanations.d: Requires a criminal conviction before the file may be used; an administrative revocation from another state is a sufficient ground on its own.

prompt: A promoter sells investors units in a vineyard it manages. Each buyer receives title to specific rows of vines, pays cash, and shares pro rata in profits from the grapes the promoter grows and markets. How are the units treated under the Howey test?

options.text: As real estate interests outside securities law, because buyers hold title to the rows
As investment contracts, because buyers rely on the promoter's efforts for profits
As agricultural commodities regulated by the CFTC rather than by state securities law
As securities if the promoter guarantees a fixed return; otherwise as real property

explanation: Under SEC v. W.J. Howey Co. (1946), an investment contract exists when there is an investment of money in a common enterprise with an expectation of profits derived from the efforts of others. Buyers here contribute cash, profits are pooled pro rata, and the promoter does the work, so the units are securities even though buyers hold title to land.

distractorExplanations.a: Howey itself involved deeded rows of citrus trees; title to land does not defeat security status when profits depend on the promoter.
distractorExplanations.c: The buyers are not trading commodity futures; they are passive investors in a managed enterprise, which is a securities question.
distractorExplanations.d: A guaranteed return is not required; the Howey test looks at expected profits from others' efforts, not at fixed payouts.

prompt: A two-year-old startup with no federal registration plans to raise $3 million solely from residents of its home state, relying on the federal intrastate exemption. Which state registration method fits the offering under the Uniform Securities Act?

options.text: Coordination, effective at the same moment the SEC declares the registration effective
Notification, which becomes effective automatically on the second business day after filing
No state registration, because the offering qualifies for a federal exemption
Qualification, effective when the Administrator orders the registration effective

explanation: Registration by coordination requires a pending federal registration, and notification (filing) is limited to established issuers with a multi-year operating and earnings history. An issuer with neither must register by qualification under USA §304, which requires full disclosure to the Administrator, and the registration becomes effective when the Administrator so orders.

distractorExplanations.a: Coordination piggybacks on a Securities Act registration statement; this issuer is not filing with the SEC at all.
distractorExplanations.b: Notification is reserved for seasoned issuers with years of continuous operation and earnings, which a two-year-old startup lacks.
distractorExplanations.c: A federal intrastate exemption removes SEC registration only; the offering still needs state registration or a state exemption.

prompt: An issuer is selling shares to accredited investors in State X under SEC Regulation D, Rule 506(b). What may the State X Administrator require for the offering?

options.text: A notice filing with a copy of Form D, a fee, and consent to service of process
Registration by qualification, since the shares are not registered with the SEC
Registration by coordination, effective once the issuer files Form D with the SEC
Merit review of the terms before sale, since accredited investors buy unregistered stock

explanation: Rule 506 offerings are federal covered securities under NSMIA, so states may not require registration or merit review. A state may still require a notice filing, generally a copy of Form D within 15 days after the first sale in the state, plus a filing fee and a consent to service of process, and it keeps its antifraud authority.

distractorExplanations.b: Lack of SEC registration does not trigger state qualification here; NSMIA preempts state registration of Rule 506 offerings.
distractorExplanations.c: Coordination applies to offerings registered under the Securities Act; filing Form D is a federal notice, not a registration statement.
distractorExplanations.d: NSMIA bars state merit review of federal covered securities, including Rule 506 offerings, regardless of who the buyers are.

prompt: Within 12 months, an issuer offers unregistered shares in State X to 8 individuals and 15 insurance companies. No commission is paid for soliciting the individuals, and the issuer reasonably believes all buyers are purchasing for investment. How does the Uniform Securities Act treat the offering?

options.text: It is not exempt, because the 23 offerees exceed the ten-offeree limit
The shares become exempt securities, so later resales are also exempt
It is an exempt private placement transaction; the shares are not exempt
It is exempt if no more than 35 of the buyers are nonaccredited investors

explanation: USA §402 exempts offers to no more than 10 persons in the state, excluding institutional investors, during 12 months if no commission is paid for soliciting noninstitutional buyers and the seller reasonably believes they buy for investment. Insurance companies are institutional, so only 8 offerees count. The exemption covers the transaction, not the security, so a later resale needs its own exemption or registration.

distractorExplanations.a: Institutional investors such as insurance companies are not counted toward the ten-offeree limit, so only 8 offerees count.
distractorExplanations.b: A transactional exemption does not make the security itself exempt; each later resale must find its own exemption or be registered.
distractorExplanations.d: The 35-purchaser figure is the federal Rule 506 cap on nonaccredited buyers; the USA private placement test counts noninstitutional offerees, not buyers.

prompt: An agent sells general obligation municipal bonds, which are exempt from state registration, and tells a client they carry a AAA rating when the actual rating is BBB. Under the Uniform Securities Act, what is the status of the agent's conduct?

It violates the antifraud rule, which applies to exempt securities as well
It becomes a violation once the client sells the bonds at a realized loss
It is an MSRB matter alone, since municipal bonds fall outside state authority

prompt: Harbor Tools common stock is listed on the New York Stock Exchange. A broker-dealer in State X plans to recommend those shares to retail clients who live in State X. Harbor Tools has not filed a registration statement with the State X Administrator. Which statement about the shares is correct?

options.text: State X cannot require registration, because these listed shares are federal covered
State X must register the shares by coordination before any retail client in the state may hear a recommendation
State X must register the shares by qualification, because these buyers are individuals rather than banks or insurers
The broker-dealer must submit the same notice filing a mutual fund submits before it may recommend the shares in State X

explanation: Common stock listed on the New York Stock Exchange is a federal covered security under the National Securities Markets Improvement Act. That status preempts state registration, so State X cannot make Harbor Tools register the shares before a broker-dealer recommends them to residents. A notice filing of the kind used for a mutual fund is not the rule for this listed common stock. The Administrator may still act if the recommendation is fraudulent.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a secondary recommendation of already listed shares with an issuer's coordinated registration; coordination tracks a federal registration statement, which these listed shares do not need.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the clients' status as individuals as a reason to register by qualification; federal covered status comes from the exchange listing, not from who the buyers are.
distractorExplanations.d: Applies the mutual-fund notice filing to exchange-listed common stock; that notice procedure fits certain federal covered funds, not this New York Stock Exchange listing.

prompt: Last month an agent filled a single unsolicited order for unlisted shares of Pine Meter, a small software firm. That order qualified as an exempt transaction. The agent now wants to telephone other clients and recommend the same shares. Pine Meter has not registered the shares in the state. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Pine Meter's shares are now an exempt security, so every later sale, including these solicited calls, is free of registration
Only that unsolicited order was exempt
The shares became federal covered once one exempt transaction was completed inside the state
The agent may solicit freely if each new buyer acknowledges in writing that the first order was unsolicited

explanation: An unsolicited nonissuer order can be an exempt transaction under the Uniform Securities Act. The exemption attaches to that order, not to Pine Meter's shares. The stock remains a nonexempt security, so telephone recommendations to other clients need registration or a separate exemption. One completed exempt transaction does not convert the shares into an exempt security, and it does not make them federal covered.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns an exempt transaction into an exempt security; the unsolicited-order exemption ends with that order and does not license a later solicitation.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an exempt transaction with federal covered status; completing one unsolicited trade does not put an unlisted software stock under federal preemption.
distractorExplanations.d: Misuses a written acknowledgment; that paper can document that an order was unsolicited, and it does not authorize the agent to solicit new buyers.

prompt: Northwind Bond Fund, an open-end investment company registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940, has completed the notice filing State X requires, including the documents filed with the SEC and a consent to service of process. The Administrator now wants to delay sales until the fund lowers its sales charge. May the Administrator impose that delay?

options.text: Yes. A completed notice filing gives the Administrator the same power to condition the offering that registration by qualification gives
Yes, but only during the fifteen days after the notice filing is received, and not after that period ends
No. The notice filing does not authorize a merit review of the sales charge
No, and the completed notice filing also waives the Administrator's antifraud authority over the fund

explanation: Shares of an investment company registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940 are federal covered securities. After Northwind completes the State X notice filing, the Administrator may not hold up sales until the sales charge is reduced. Notice filing is not merit review and it is not registration by qualification. Antifraud authority remains if the fund misstates that charge. A notice filing does not exempt the fund from the antifraud rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a notice filing with qualification; qualification lets an Administrator decide effectiveness, and a federal covered fund is not registered that way.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents a fifteen-day merit window; the time allowed to submit a notice is not permission to delay sales over the size of the sales charge.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats completion of a notice filing as an exemption from the antifraud rule; the Administrator can still pursue a material misstatement about the charge.

prompt: A registered agent sells U.S. Treasury notes to a State X client. Those notes are exempt from registration under the Uniform Securities Act. The agent tells the client the notes are guaranteed by the client's city. That statement is false. How does the Act treat the agent's statement?

options.text: As outside the Act, because an exempt security is not subject to state securities law at all
As lawful, because an exemption from registration is also an exemption from the antifraud rule
As a violation only if the client later sells the notes and realizes a loss on the trade
As an antifraud violation, which still covers this exempt security

explanation: Uniform Securities Act antifraud provisions apply to the offer and sale of any security. U.S. Treasury notes are exempt from state registration, and that exemption does not excuse a false statement. Telling the client the notes are guaranteed by the city is an untrue statement of a material fact. An exemption from registration is not an exemption from the antifraud rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a registration exemption as a repeal of the Act; Treasury notes need not be registered, and fraud in selling them is still unlawful.
distractorExplanations.b: Equates an exemption from registration with an exemption from the antifraud rule; the Act keeps fraud liability for exempt securities.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds a realized-loss condition the Act does not require; the false city guarantee is unlawful when made, whether or not the client later sells.

prompt: Dana asks her agent to buy two contracts from the same insurer: a fixed annuity that credits a guaranteed rate, and a variable annuity whose payments depend on securities in a separate account. Under the Uniform Securities Act, which contract is a security?

options.text: Only the variable annuity
Only the fixed annuity, because a guaranteed credited rate is what makes an insurance contract a security
Both contracts, because each one is issued by an insurance company and offered through an agent for a premium
Neither contract, because the Act excludes every product an insurance company issues from the definition of a security

explanation: A fixed annuity is an insurance product, not a security. The insurer stands behind a guaranteed credited rate, and the buyer does not take market risk in a pool of securities. A variable annuity is a security because the owner bears investment risk and the payments move with the separate account. Issuance by an insurance company does not remove the variable contract from the definition of a security.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the two products; the guaranteed rate is a reason the fixed annuity is insurance, not a reason it is a security.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the insurer's identity as decisive; a fixed annuity and a variable annuity are classified separately even when one company issues both.
distractorExplanations.d: Overreads the insurance exclusion; variable annuities remain securities even though an insurance company issues the contract.

prompt: Before a corporation is formed, a promoter takes subscription agreements from seven State X residents for its common stock. No subscriber pays any money, the promoter is paid no commission, and no other person is solicited. How does the Uniform Securities Act classify these subscriptions?

options.text: As exempt securities, so the promoter may collect the full purchase price now and buyers may resell freely without registration
As an exempt transaction, not as an exempt security
As a federal covered security, because the subscriptions were signed before the corporation existed
As unlawful offers, because no subscription may be taken until a registration statement is already effective

explanation: A preorganization subscription is an exempt transaction when the number of subscribers does not exceed ten, no commission is paid for soliciting them, and no subscriber makes a payment. These seven residents fit that transaction exemption. The common stock is not an exempt security, and it is not federal covered merely because the company is not yet formed. The promoter still may not collect the purchase money until the shares are registered or another exemption applies.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an exempt transaction with an exempt security; fitting the subscription exemption does not let buyers pay now or resell the stock as if it were exempt.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a not-yet-formed issuer as a federal covered security; that status comes from a listing, a registered fund, or a specified federal offering, not from this timing.
distractorExplanations.d: Ignores the preorganization exemption; subscriptions can be taken before effectiveness when the subscriber limit, no-commission condition, and no-payment condition are met.

prompt: A factory wants to issue promissory notes that mature in 270 days and are sold in denominations of $25,000. The notes are rated in one of the three highest categories, and the proceeds will pay for inventory. Do these notes qualify for the Uniform Securities Act's commercial-paper exemption?

options.text: Yes. Inventory financing alone makes any promissory note an exempt security, whatever the maturity or the denomination
Yes. The 270-day maturity and the top rating are enough, so the $25,000 denomination does not affect the exemption
No. The $25,000 denomination is below the $50,000 minimum
No. Commercial paper is excluded from the definition of a security, so no exemption analysis applies to these notes

explanation: The commercial-paper exemption covers a note used for a current transaction, such as inventory, only when the note also matures in nine months or less and is issued in denominations of at least $50,000, with a rating in one of the three highest categories. A 270-day maturity sits inside nine months, and the rating test is met, but $25,000 is short of $50,000. These notes therefore are not exempt under that provision.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at the current-transaction use; inventory financing does not drop the nine-month maturity test or the $50,000 denomination test.
distractorExplanations.b: Drops the denomination test; a 270-day maturity and a top-three rating still fail when each note is only $25,000.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an exemption with an exclusion; notes that miss this exemption remain securities and still need registration or a different exemption.

prompt: Pellican Industries common stock is listed on the New York Stock Exchange. Pellican will issue debentures that rank senior to that common stock, and the debentures will not be listed. An agent tells a State X client the debentures must be registered by qualification because only the common stock is listed. The agent is

options.text: Correct. Qualification is required for every class the issuer sells whenever that class is not itself listed on the exchange
Correct, unless the debentures are sold only to a bank, because a bank buyer erases any need to analyze the listing
Incorrect. The debentures are exempt securities for every buyer solely because the issuer already has common stock outstanding
Incorrect. A security senior to that listed common stock is federal covered too

Pellican's debentures qualify even though the debentures themselves are not listed. State X cannot require registration by qualification. The agent was wrong to stop the analysis at the listed common stock. Antifraud provisions still apply to the debenture sale.

distractorExplanations.a: Limits federal covered status to the listed class; a senior debenture of the same issuer is federal covered without its own exchange listing.
distractorExplanations.b: Substitutes a bank-buyer exemption for the listing rule; seniority to the listed common stock is what makes these debentures federal covered.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents an exempt-security status from the mere existence of common stock; the debentures are federal covered because they rank senior to a listed class.

prompt: During the past year, Red Clay Mills offered its unregistered common stock only to nine State X residents. Each resident is an accredited investor under federal standards. Red Clay paid no commission, contacted no bank or insurance company, and reasonably believes every buyer is purchasing for investment. Which statement is correct?

options.text: This can be an exempt transaction, and the stock is not an exempt security
This cannot use the state limited-offering exemption, because accredited investors are left out of the person count and only institutions may buy
The stock is federal covered solely because every offeree meets the accredited-investor test under federal standards
The stock is now an exempt security, so a later offer to the general public in State X needs no registration or exemption

explanation: The Uniform Securities Act limited-offering exemption is an exempt transaction. It allows offers to no more than ten persons in twelve months, other than institutional investors, if no commission is paid to solicit those persons and the seller reasonably believes they are buying for investment. An accredited individual is still one person in that count. Nine residents are within ten, so the exemption can apply. Accreditation alone does not make the shares federal covered, and this transaction exemption does not make the stock an exempt security.

distractorExplanations.b: Misstates the count; accredited individuals are not institutions, so they are included among the persons, and nine of them can still fit the exemption.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an accredited buyer with a federal covered security; selling to accredited residents does not, by itself, create federal preemption of state registration.
distractorExplanations.d: Turns an exempt transaction into an exempt security; a later public offer is a new transaction and is not carried by this limited offering.

prompt: A mining founder gives her nephew a certificate for assessable stock in the company and receives nothing in return. The company can later assess the shares and require the nephew to pay more. Under the Uniform Securities Act, this gift is

options.text: Not a sale, because a transfer between relatives involves no value and assessable shares are ordinary personal property
A sale, because the shares can require a later payment
Not a sale unless the nephew actually pays an assessment in the same month the certificate is delivered
An exempt security, because a family gift is excluded from the definition of a security under the Act

explanation: The Uniform Securities Act treats a gift of assessable stock as a sale. No cash changes hands today, but the nephew can be required to pay an assessment later, so the delivery is for value. A gift of nonassessable stock would not be a sale. The family relationship does not make the shares an exempt security, and a false statement about the shares can still violate the antifraud rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores the assessment; the possibility of a later required payment is the value that makes this gift a sale, and kinship does not erase it.
distractorExplanations.c: Waits for the assessment to be collected; the Act treats the gift of assessable stock as a sale when the certificate is delivered, not only after a later bill is paid.
distractorExplanations.d: Calls a family gift an exempt security; the delivery is a sale of a security, and neither the relationship nor the word gift creates an exemption from registration.

prompt: Grayline Manufacturing sells a block of newly issued common stock to its managing underwriter in a firm-commitment deal. That issuer-to-underwriter trade is an exempt transaction. The underwriter next offers the same shares to public customers in State X. The shares are not listed, not federal covered, and not otherwise exempt. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The underwriter exemption follows the shares into the public offer, so State X customers may buy them with no registration

Only the sale to the underwriter was exempt; the public offer is not

distractorExplanations.a: Extends the underwriter exemption to the retail distribution; that exemption covers the issuer-to-underwriter trade and not the later public offer.
distractorExplanations.b: Turns an exempt transaction into an exempt security; the underwriter's purchase does not change the registration status of the common stock itself.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a firm-commitment purchase with federal covered status; a listing, a registered fund, or a specified federal offering creates that status, and this purchase does not.

prompt: Under the NASAA model rule on IAR registration requirements, which applicant satisfies the IAR qualification examination requirement without passing another exam?

distractorExplanations.c: A CPA license alone is not on the model rule's waiver list; a CPA needs the PFS credential or must pass the qualifying exam.

prompt: Mara Chen is a partner at a state-registered adviser. She never meets a client. Each week she approves which model portfolios the client-facing staff may recommend. Under the Uniform Securities Act, which statement is correct?

She must register with the SEC as a federal covered representative, because a partner who approves models is not a state IAR
